en: For by the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous, kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are by sacrifices. (8.311)

Men joined with evil are sinful; their restraint has been described previously. Those who act according to the scriptures are virtuous; their gathering, favoring, and assistance according to one's ability [constitute their purification]. By this they are purified—that is, they become free from sin—as if by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*); this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Alternatively, "purification" is simply the non-arising of sin, as for Brahmins through constant sacrifices, namely the obligatory great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) and so forth. (8.311)
A lord who seeks his own welfare should always forgive those men who bring lawsuits against him, as well as children, the elderly, and the sick. (8.312)

The "parties" are the plaintiff, the defendant, their relatives, and their friends. If, while someone is being executed, his father or mother should revile, abuse, or curse the king, then forgiveness must be exercised; this applies even to children and others who are parties to the case. In this way, one’s own welfare is accomplished. That "one must be patient"—this very injunction has as its fruit one’s own welfare. (8.312)
He who, when reviled by those in distress, endures it with patience, is exalted in heaven because of that;
but he who, out of pride in his power, does not endure it, goes to hell because of that. (8.313)

When one who has been struck by those in distress, or reviled and abused by those unrelated to him, endures this and does not become angry, he is exalted in heaven by that very act of forbearance. [The suffix *yaḥ* is used here because the root belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* class. He attains greatness in heaven. Therefore, forbearance should be practiced without anger. Since one who is free from desire acts according to his will, the author says: however, when one does not endure out of the conceit of thinking "I am the master," he goes to hell. The mention of "those in distress" is intended to include children and the elderly as well, as this is a supplement to what preceded. (8.313)
The wise thief should go before the king with disheveled hair, confessing that theft: "I am a man of such deeds; punish me. (8.314)

When no specific qualification is mentioned, the thief to be regarded as a stealer of gold is the one for whom the act of going [to the king] is prescribed in another scriptural text. This is not an injunction regarding the act of coming, because it is a rule concerning punishment. For it has been stated: "Therefore, I shall proclaim the rule for a thief in the determination of punishment" (MDh 8.301). Thus, the mention of going here is a restatement (anuvāda). A stealer of gold must go into the presence of the king with disheveled hair, being wise and courageous. There is an alternative reading, "running" (*dhāvatā*). Proclaiming that sin on the road, he should say: "I am a doer of such a deed; this much gold was stolen by me from a Brāhmaṇa; inflict punishment upon me. (8.314)
Taking up a club or a staff made of khadira wood, or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron rod. (8.315)
Some maintain that there is an instruction regarding the clubs and other implements according to the sequence of the social classes (*varṇas*).

That is incorrect; for the word "or" (*vā*) would not be justified. Furthermore, they do not accept this as an expiation for a Brāhmaṇa; we shall examine those expiations in their proper place. A staff made of *khadira* wood is simply a stick; it is not to be used in conjunction with a mace (*muśala*). (8.315)
Whether by punishment or by release, the thief is freed from his theft;
but if the king does not punish him, he incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.316)

By punishing with clubs and other weapons, a Kṣatriya or others are released from sin; this is because of *vimokṣa*, which means release or abandonment. [The text says: "Go, you are forgiven," for it is stated that "the Brāhmaṇa is purified by austerity alone" (MDh 11.99). Thus, both execution and austerity are prescribed. Among these, execution is not permitted for a Brāhmaṇa; rather, austerity serves as his penance (*prāyaścitta*). Furthermore, there is no requirement for the king to approach [the Brāhmaṇa] at his own will regarding austerity. Therefore, this release applies to Kṣatriyas and others, and that occurs after the king has taken a monetary fine. For this reason, he says "without having punished," and so forth. Nor does the fault accrue to the king merely because of failing to punish when purification through release has occurred. Nor can it be argued: "Punishment is prescribed and release is also prescribed; therefore, the statement regarding the fault refers to the alternative where punishment is applied. For such an interpretation would make the rule optional (*pākṣika*), and it is not proper to assume that what is heard as an obligatory (*nitya*) injunction is merely optional. Accordingly, Vasiṣṭha and others have stated this in general terms.

"He overtakes the king who releases a criminal; if the king should have him executed, he incurs no fault by acting according to dharma. (VaDh 19.46) This alternative is not tenable. For in some cases this injury is prohibited: "One shall not harm living beings," which is obtained as a human duty through passion and so forth. In other cases it is enjoined for the sake of the sacrifice: "He who is initiated [should offer] that which belongs to Agni and Soma" (TS 6.1.11.6). But this statement regarding the release from punishment cannot indeed be an injunction when there is already a prohibition.
How is it that there is no prohibition? For the general prohibition, "One must not harm living beings," cannot be set aside without a specific injunction.

Now, if it is argued: "This is not the scope of the prohibition, because it is for the sake of ritual action (karma)," then how can its being for the sake of ritual action be understood without an injunction? If you say, "From worldly convention," then the activity is merely worldly. How, then, could the prohibition apply to that?

But surely, let the engagement with the primary act (*pradhāna*) be examined. If it is an engagement based on Vedic injunction (*vaidikī pravṛtti*), then since the subsidiary (*aṅga*) is part of that [primary], the violence (*hiṃsā*) therein must also stem from that very same source; for there is indeed one and the same engagement for both the subsidiary and the primary. If, on the other hand, the engagement with the subsidiary arises from a desire for gain (*lipsā*), then this violence is all the more worldly (*laukikī*). For the restriction regarding the duty of protecting subjects for one seeking a livelihood is not a Vedic injunction. Therefore, even though this violence resides in a subsidiary act, because it is equal to the *śyena* sacrifice, it falls within the scope of prohibition. Moreover, its status as a subsidiary is not fixed as something worldly; for the protection of subjects cannot be accomplished without violence—since it can also be accomplished through restraint and other means—this is not a rule. If the engagement with both the subsidiary and the primary were of a single uniform nature, then there would be no distinction between the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice and the *śyena* sacrifice by virtue of this [rule]. Therefore, even if the primary act is characterized by desire for gain, it must be admitted that the subsidiary is characterized by a Vedic injunction (*vidhilakṣaṇa*). Yet, it is impossible to admit that this violence is characterized by a Vedic injunction, because its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its function (*kārya*) are worldly, as are the act of protection and the violence itself. If, however, it were characterized by a Vedic injunction, it would have to be subject to option (*vikalpitum arhati*) like the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, and thus it would be prohibited by the words of the sacred teaching (*śāsana*).

Others, however, hold this view: these are two distinct statements. By the words "because of the command," the intention of the thief is expressed; by the subsequent half-verse, the fault incurred by the king for failing to issue that command is stated. In that case, if the king, having accepted the fault of not commanding upon himself, were to release him, he would indeed be liberated from the sin. Likewise, even for a Brāhmaṇa who has come forward of his own accord, execution is a cause of purification, based on the statement: "He is the target of those who bear weapons" (MDh 11.72). Furthermore, according to the rule "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 12.43), if the king should kill him despite the prohibition, the Brāhmaṇa would still be purified.
Without having punished him with clubs and the like, and without having killed him, he becomes joined with whatever sin belongs to the thief. (8.316)
The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife to her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer to their teacher; and a thief to the king. (8.317)

One who eats food is an *annāda*. A killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahā*) is a killer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*). He who eats the food belonging to such a person "wipes off" (*mārṣṭi*), that is, casts away or transfers, that sin of killing a Brahmin onto himself. Just as a dirty cloth is wiped in water and its dirt is transferred there, so it is here. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*); that sin arises for him, but the sin of the Brahmin-killer does not perish [by that act]. In the case of a wife who is unfaithful—that is, one who has a lover—if her husband forgives her, the sin is produced for the husband; it does not depart from her. In the case of a teacher, both the pupil and the sacrificer may offend the teacher by rising before the sun at dawn and other such transgressions. While the teacher forgives, he casts that sin upon himself. Likewise, the sacrificer [casts his sin] upon the officiating priest (*yājaka*). Since the priest is also a "teacher," the term "officiating priest" was not mentioned separately. Similarly, a thief [casts his sin] upon the king, provided he is not punished by the king. Even a sacrificer, when the ritual has commenced, may deviate from the rule if he does not abide by the word of the officiating priest; in that case, he should be abandoned, but one must not subject him to beating and the like as one would a pupil. One should not think that there is a formal rule (*vidhi*) regarding all these cases, such as the eaters of food and so forth; therefore, this is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). (8.317)
But men who have committed sins, having been punished by kings, go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds. (8.318)

This clarifies what was said regarding how those who perform actions protect themselves when punishing evildoers: those upon whom punishment has been imposed and inflicted by kings, having committed sins, become stainless and free from sin through the king's restraint. When sin has departed, they attain heaven by means of that karma of theirs which leads to the ascent to heaven. For great sin is an obstacle to the fruit of pure action. [The term] *sukṛtinaḥ* refers to those who constantly perform good deeds, just like the virtuous and righteous (*dhārmika*). Unrighteousness (*adharma*) does not arise for the wicked; rather, that which had arisen in them is destroyed by restraint—this is the distinction between prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).

Because of the mention of "human beings" (*mānava*) and because of the context, this does not refer exclusively to thieves. Furthermore, the word "punishment" (*daṇḍa*) refers to physical restraint and does not overstep the context. For a monetary fine is for the sake of the king; it is indeed the king's livelihood. However, regarding corporal punishment, its purpose being for the sake of the one being punished cannot be denied, for that is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the skin. Now, if this thought occurs: "Protection itself cannot be accomplished without violence, and since that [protection] is for the sake of the king, how can the killing have the purpose of the one being killed?"—then why is it denied that protection is seen to be for the sake of the one being protected? Indeed, that kingdom is not something to be acquired by the king solely for his own self-preservation; rather, servants are employed through taxes, tolls, and so forth. Therefore, since protection is even more dependent upon [the presence of] violence, the fact that violence has the purpose of the one being harmed is not established. Or how is it that protection is not accomplished without violence? If they are restrained for this very purpose [of protection], they will simply commit the forbidden act again; they can be controlled even by means of imprisonment and the like. Or, if it is argued that seeing those who have been restrained, others will not engage in such acts out of fear—and thus [the king] can cause them suffering even with a monetary fine—then even when thousands are being killed, people continue to engage in the act. Therefore, this violence, while being for the sake of protection, must be understood as a refinement of the one being harmed. Consequently, there is a restriction regarding the cutting off of hands and other limbs. Moreover, the rules concerning elephants and so forth will produce invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*) only for the ones being punished; it will not be for the sake of the king.

Therefore, it is established that for those who commit sins, liberation from punishment comes through corporal punishment and not through a fine of wealth. Accordingly, the author will later prescribe branding for those guilty of mortal sins (*mahāpātakin*)—even after they have been deprived of all their property and their punishment has been cast into the water—for the purpose of excluding them from social intercourse. Furthermore, if they were purified by a fine of wealth, then branding would be rendered useless.

Moreover, as for the distinction between one who comes of his own accord and one who is brought [as a prisoner], let that distinction apply only to the thief himself (as specified in verse 8.320). All this, however, pertains to the subject of corporal punishment. (8.318)
But he who takes a rope or a water-pot from a well, or who breaks a public water-shed, shall receive a fine of one māṣa and must restore that [item] to its place. (8.319)

A *prapā* is a place where people drink; it is either a reservoir for water or a vessel containing drawn-up water. The specific species of bean (*māṣa*) is not specified here; it should be understood as belonging to the categories of desert, arid, or marshy lands. And one should collect such [rope and so forth] and give it at that place, not to the king. (8.319)
For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he shall be made to pay eleven times its value, and that property shall be returned to its owner. (8.320)

The word *kumbha* refers to a specific measure and not merely to a jar; its determination varies by region, being twenty *prasthas* in some places and twenty-two in others. For one who steals more than ten [measures], the rule regarding corporal punishment has been stated, and it is regulated by the nature of the offense (*anubandha*) and other factors. For the remaining ten measures, the standard fine is elevenfold. The principle that "that [stolen property] belongs to him [the owner]" is to be applied everywhere in cases of theft. It is recorded in the Smṛtis that grain consists of seventeen types, such as rice, barley, and so forth. (8.320)
Likewise, for goods measured by weight, such as gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the finest garments, there shall be the death penalty when the amount exceeds one hundred.

*Dharaṇa* means weight (*dharimā*), that is, a scale; those things measured or determined by it are *dharmameya*. Since liquids such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) are measured by *prastha* and other units, whereas solids are measured by weight, he specifies "gold, silver, and so forth" for this purpose. Although silver is already included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is mentioned again specifically to include coral and similar items through their inclusion under "scale-measure," but not copper, iron, and the like. For stealing more than one hundred of these, the punishment is death. But what constitutes this "one hundred"—is it *pala*s, or *karṣa*s, or perhaps *kārṣāpaṇa*s?

Some say "of *palas*," but there is no specific reason for this [restriction]. Therefore, in whatever place, at the time of weighing goods, the conventional usage is by a certain number—such as "this is a hundred of gold"—whether measured in *tolakas* or in *palas*, the determination is according to local custom.

And regarding the best garments, such as silk (*kauśeya*) and brocade (*paṭṭa*), etc.—the connection is that "if exceeding one hundred, there is death. Here too, a pair of garments is counted as one; however, a bed-cover made of flowers and so forth is counted as only one.
But surely, since [the definition] is already established by the words "of gold, silver, and so forth," the inclusion of the term "measurable" (parimeya) is redundant.

This is not meaningless, as it is for the purpose of including highly valuable items such as camphor, agallochum, musk, and so forth. By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), metallic objects are included, or those designated by measures such as the *niṣka*. For there is no designation of camphor and the like in terms of *karṣa* and similar weights. Even though, as with gold, the number one hundred may apply to silver as well, nevertheless, just as there is a distinction in penance, a distinction in punishment is also appropriate, because it is unjust to treat unequal things as equal. Therefore, when silver is taken that has a value equal to that of gold, there is the death penalty. However, in the case of camphor and the like, the number one hundred applies only to *pala* units. (8.321)
But for stealing more than fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remainder, however, one should determine a fine eleven times the value. 8.322.

This is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "from its value": it is not only the stolen object itself that must be given; for in some cases, an item of that same kind may simply not be obtainable. Therefore, restitution may be made by means of coins or grain and the like. (8.322)
For the abduction of men of noble birth, and especially women, as well as for the theft of principal gems, one deserves the death penalty. (8.323)

Those born into noble families who possess qualities such as learning are *kulīna* (of noble birth). The meaning is that this refers especially to women who are endowed with virtue, beauty, and good fortune. Because of the word *ca* ("and"), it follows that they must also be of noble birth; the qualifications for women are to be understood in mutual dependence [with one another]. "Principal" means the most excellent, such as diamonds, lapis lazuli, emeralds, and so forth. Here too, the phrase "equal to a hundred pieces of gold" is to be supplied. Otherwise, excellence would be merely relative, and the punishment would not be fixed. He deserves death. In all cases, the sense of "deserving" (*arhati*) should be applied with due regard for the consequences (*anubandha*) and other factors. For those who are not of noble birth, the remaining ones, and those who are not principal, the rule is simply: "But in the case of the remainder, elevenfold" (MDh 8.322). 8.323.
In cases of the theft of large cattle, weapons, or medicine, the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the purpose. 8.324.

Large animals refer to elephants, horses, and the like. In cases of their theft, the determination of punishment takes into account the time and the purpose [of the act]. But is it not true that consideration of time and other factors is stated for all cases? Indeed, it is said: "One should consider the time, place, age, and capacity when determining the application of punishments" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.279).

True. Once the nature of the punishment has been determined, its degree—whether it be lesser or greater—depends on factors such as the consequences (*anubandha*). For example, in the case of a rule prescribing death, there is a consideration of whether the penalty should be flogging, execution, or something else. Here, however, the punishment is of an entirely different character. For instance, even a sword worth twenty *paṇas*, if stolen from an enemy who has his weapon raised, results in the penalty of death because of the gravity of that act and the timing; at other times, the fine would be double or elevenfold. Likewise, if a medicine of great utility is stolen at the very moment it is needed, or if it is stolen while being prepared—requiring decoctions and the like—and by the lapse of time causes great suffering to the patient, then the punishment is severe. At other times, however, it is small. No such disparity could be found without these intervening circumstances. Otherwise, this single verse alone would have sufficed for the entire section on punishments. Therefore, this must be explained: during a state of war, the punishment for horses and the like depends on the needs of the kingdom; for weapons used by the king, there may sometimes be leniency and sometimes a heavy fine. But for cattle, buffaloes, and so forth belonging to the subjects, the king must not show leniency. Furthermore, the specific purpose served by the horses and other items must also be taken into account. Even regarding war, if it takes place in a mountainous region where horses are of little use, there is indeed a reduction in the punishment.

Having reached the appropriate time, having understood it, and having examined it, one should determine the punishment; for in this matter, that [the king] alone has the power, not the scripture. 8.324.
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, for breaking a stable, and likewise for the theft of livestock, one must immediately have half a foot amputated. (8.325)

"Belonging to Brahmins" means dependent upon Brahmins or owned by Brahmins. The locative case here has the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhy-arthe saptamī*); thus, "in the case of the theft of those [cows]. Regarding "animals," such as goats, sheep, and so forth—the plural number is not intended to be restrictive in every instance. "Immediately" means at that very moment, without deliberation. "Half-foot" (*ardha-pāda*) means half of a foot; one who possesses that is "half-footed" (*ardha-pādika*). And this is possible if half of a foot is cut off by it. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that "cutting off half a foot must be performed. "Kharikā" is that by which a bull is driven in a cow-cart, a field, and so forth. "In the case of piercing" means causing pain with a goad while the animal is being driven.

The predecessors explain that "breaking" (bhedana) is intended as an illustration for driving [animals]. One who drives them necessarily causes them pain. Others read: "This penalty applies specifically when driving with a goad.

Still others say that the fourth part of the foot, the hindquarter, is called *kharikā*. Regarding this *kharikā*, if a herdsman or anyone else breaks one that is known to be prone to running away, he should be made to pay half a *pāda* fine.
Others, however, taking the locative case as indicating the location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), supply words such as "curd and so forth stored in a cow-pen."
That is incorrect; since the connection with the words actually heard is possible, why resort to textual supplementation (adhyāhāra)? || 8.325 ||
Of thread, cotton, and fermenting agents; of cow dung and molasses; of curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass. || 8.326 ||
For the theft of vessels made of bamboo or split cane, as well as salts, and likewise for the theft of earthenware, clay, or ashes; || 8.327 ||
Of fish, of birds, of oil, of clarified butter, of meat, of honey, and whatever else is derived from animals. (8.328)
For other such items as these, for raw grain, for cooked rice, and for all kinds of cooked food, the fine shall be double their value. (8.329)

*Ūrṇāsaṇa* and the like refer to woolen cloth and so forth. *Lavaṇa* refers to salts such as rock salt (*saindhava*) and black salt (*biḍalavaṇa*). And whatever else originates from animals, such as meat and the like; and other items such as cakes (*apūpa*), sweetmeats (*modaka*), and so on. The word "and the like" (*ādi*) indicates a category (*prakāra*). A category consists of similarity, likeness, or equality, in the form of performing similar functions, utility, and so forth. Thus, clarified butter scum (*sarpirmaṇḍa*), sugarcane pieces (*ikṣukhaṇḍa*), sugar (*śarkarā*), inspissated milk (*kilāṭa*), thickened milk (*kūrcikā*), and the like are included among the cakes. Some also maintain that what originates from animals includes the wool of the *rāṅkava* deer and horses, and so on. By the inclusion of "and the like," both the primary substance (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*) are intended. Furthermore, the separate mention of "curd and milk" is for the sake of illustration. Similarly, by the mention of "wool," clothing made of wool is also included. Although reed-mats (*nalika*) and the like are made of wool, because they originate from animals and are of superior quality, they fall under the scope of the exception stated as "and those of the superior. The word "oil" (*taila*) denotes oily substances in general, not only the modification of sesame seeds. Therefore, linseed oil, *priyaṅgu* oil, castor oil (*pañcāṅgula*), and others are also included. (8.326–29)
For flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
and other unhusked plants, the fine shall be five kṛṣṇalas.

The flowers are those such as the *navamālikā* and others. "Green" refers to unripe grain standing in the field. "Mountains" refers to trees. Regarding the phrase "in others that have not been winnowed," because the plural number implies that winnowing—which consists of the removal of husks, straw, and so forth—is possible only in the case of grains, the mention of "grain" (*dhānya*) alone is drawn forward from the subsequent verse. For even though shrubs and the like possess foliage, and flowers likewise possess it, there is no conventional usage of the term "winnowed" (*paripūta*) for them. The seventh [case-ending] is used in relation to the act of taking away.

That [penalty], however, follows from the preceding [rule]. Here, the fine is five *kṛṣṇalas*. *Kṛṣṇalas* are made of various substances, depending on whether the purpose requires a small or large quantity. "Of gold," according to the predecessors. (8.330)

When grain, vegetables, roots, or fruits have been cleaned, the fine shall be one hundred panas for those who act without prior notice, and fifty panas as a penalty for those who act with notice. (8.331)

The *mūla* consists of sugarcane, grapes, and the like. Regarding "theft without conciliation" (*niranvaye dravyaharaṇe*): *anvaya* means conciliation, that is, the application of affection and so forth toward the owner, such as saying, "What is yours is indeed mine"—acting with this mindset—or speaking words such as, "If it is not so, then please take it back. Where such [conciliatory acts] are not performed, that is "without conciliation" (*niranvaya*). Because it is a form of violence (*sāhasa*), the punishment is more severe. "With conciliation" (*sānvaya*) means together with conciliation.

Alternatively, "without connection" (*niranvaya*) means that there is no relationship whatsoever with anyone, such as living in the same village; for that reason, he shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]. Alternatively, "without connection" means unprotected. However, when a protector exists, the fine is small because the fault is shared by both parties. This penalty applies to grains situated in threshing floors, for it is there that they are stored. But in the case of those situated in houses, the elevenfold fine has been stated previously (cf. MDh 8.320). || 8.331 ||

An act committed by force, provided it is accompanied by a claim of ownership, is *sāhasa* (robbery); whereas taking property without such a claim and then denying it constitutes *steya* (theft). 8.332.

The taking away of another’s property is called theft (*steya*); and by virtue of the established meaning of the verbal root, the agent of this very act is a thief (*stena*). However, since this specific legal designation is intended here, this verse is for that purpose. Theft is not merely the taking of another’s property, because otherwise the penalty for theft would undesirably apply even to cases such as the non-payment of debts or the misappropriation of deposits. The distinction in terminology is for the sake of a distinction in punishment.

Action that causes suffering to others includes tearing clothes, setting fire [to property], stealing goods, and so forth. Even though there is no actual theft of goods when setting fire [to them], they consider it indeed to be theft because it is done in secret and because of the concealment [of the act]. For in the case of theft, the punishment depends on the specific nature of the object; that [specificity] would not apply here [if it were not considered theft]. It is for this very reason that [the act of arson] is elevated to the section on theft (*steya*). By using the term "action" (*karma*) in the phrase "violent action" (*prasabhaṃ karma*), it is indicated that even if it is something other than the theft of goods, anything else done in such a manner improperly constitutes *sāhasa* (violence). What, then, is the punishment for setting fire and so forth when it is done without violence? We shall explain this under the section on the removal of thorns (*kaṇṭakaśuddhi*). For this very reason, they prescribe a punishment in the removal of thorns for breaking into a house (*saṃdhiccheda*), even though there may be no theft of goods; otherwise, it would have been mentioned simply as theft. (8.332)
But the king shall fine that man one hundred [paṇas] who steals these prepared materials, as well as he who would steal the fire from the house. (8.333)

These items, such as thread and the like, are either "prepared" (*upakḷpta*), meaning they are ready for the time of use such as giving or wearing; or "refined" (*saṃskṛta*), meaning their functional capacity has been enhanced. For example, that very same thread, when placed in the hands of a weaver for the purpose of weaving, is sometimes doubled and sometimes twisted. Similarly, there is the refinement of curd by churning, or milk by adding black pepper, sugar, and so forth; likewise, the refinement of milk into ghee and the like. In such cases, the fine is one hundred [paṇas]. If the reading is *ādyam* (the first), it refers to the first *sāhasa* fine. Regarding fire: taking it from a fire-sanctuary (*agnigṛha*) is for the purpose of the domestic fire-sacrifice (*śālāgnihotra*) and so on; or, during winter, providing fire—even if not formally maintained—to the poor who are afflicted by the cold, either at the time of cooking or at the time of warming to ward off the cold and other discomforts. This penalty for fire applies without distinction whether the fire is small or large, prepared or unprepared.

Even though the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) is included in the mention of "the staff for the Sūtra and others" (MDh 8.326), a fine based on the value of fire (*agni*) is not possible, because the practice of buying and selling it is not established. Rather, a fine twice the value of that fuel by which a fire of a certain measure is produced, or twice the value of those sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) [required for its re-establishment], is possible; it can indeed be designated, and the satisfaction of the owner remains intact. Therefore, in the case of stealing the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*), the owner must be compensated for as much as is required for the rite of re-consecration (*punar-ādheya*) and the expiatory sacrifice (*prāyaścittīṣṭi*). Consequently, this fine for fire applies only to the *śālāpraṇītāgni* (the fire brought into the hall), because it is of small value; but in the case of the *tretāgni*, it is twice its value. Thus, when materials used as auxiliaries for sacrifices—which are easily available and do not terminate one's qualification [to perform rites]—are stolen, Śaṅkha states: "For one who steals *kuśa* grass, water-pots, or materials for the *agnihotra*, there shall be amputation of a limb. However, when the fires themselves are stolen, the very qualification [to perform rites] ceases. In that case, how could there not be a heavy punishment? (8.333)
With whatever limb a thief commits an offense against men, that very limb the king shall take away as a deterrent. (8.334)

This punishment applies to one who persists in the offense again and again. For one who, even when punished with a fine, does not abide by the path, and who—having been punished three or four times—still does not desist, there shall be the amputation of a limb; this is independent of the type or quantity of the property involved, and independent of whether it was a burglary or another form of theft. Whatever limb the thief relies upon for strength while persisting in his thievery—that very limb the king shall take away or cut off. If someone, relying on the strength of his feet and using them to flee, thinks, "No one at all is able to follow me," his feet shall be cut off. Another, thinking, "I am an expert in breaking through walls," shall have his hands cut off. *Pratyādeśa* means to show a corresponding result [as a warning]. It is either a humiliating treatment characterized by self-assertion, pride, anger, and contempt, or it is a public declaration intended to explain: "Whoever acts in such a way, I shall treat him in this same manner. (8.334)
Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest—there is no one who, failing to abide by his own duty, is beyond the king's punishment. (8.335)

"Wife and son are one's own body" (MDh 4.184); that is, one's own physical self. But what is punishment for the self? It refers to penance, austerity, giving of wealth, and so forth. One who has deviated from his own dharma—whosoever does not practice his own duty, all such persons are subject to punishment. (8.335)
Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, the king should be fined one thousand; such is the established rule. (8.336)

An ordinary person is a common man who is not endowed with exceptional virtues. For him, whatever fine is prescribed for a particular offense, that same fine shall be multiplied a thousandfold for the king; this is because the mention of the *kārṣāpaṇa* is intended as an illustration of the scale of the fine, and because punishment serves a visible purpose. Furthermore, since it is impossible to restrain another without first restraining oneself, it is logical that the king deserves a proportionate punishment for his own transgressions. Because he possesses great wealth, he should not disregard even a small fine. By this same principle, the relative degree of fines for those authorized by the king—such as ministers, domestic priests, and others—is determined. And the monetary fine for Brahmins should be disposed of either by casting it into the waters or offering it to Varuṇa; for the author will state later: "For he is the wielder of the rod of punishment for kings" (MDh 9.245). [8.336]
For a Śūdra, however, the guilt in the case of theft becomes eightfold;
for a Vaiśya it is sixteenfold, and for a Kṣatriya it is thirty-twofold. (8.337)
For a Brahmin, it may be sixty-four, or even a full hundred;
or it may be double that sixty-four, for he indeed knows both their faults and virtues. (8.338)

Because he is one who knows both the faults and virtues [of others], this is the punishment for the learned; where a base person is made to pay one *kārṣāpaṇa*, there a learned Śūdra is fined eightfold. That which is incurred or connected with—namely, the guilt or sin—is thus called [an *aṣṭāpada*]. Or, it is that by which one is struck or multiplied; in either sense, the word *aṣṭāpada* denotes an eightfold amount. Likewise, that same fine is doubled for a Vaiśya, for he is directly entitled to study and knowledge. A Śūdra, however, might somehow acquire some knowledge through his dependence on or association with Brāhmaṇas. But a Kṣatriya, due to the duty of protection, is punished with double that even though his learning is equal, because of the fault inherent in his office. As for a Brāhmaṇa, the lawgiver is not satisfied with a mere fine; rather, it is sixty-four, or one hundred and twenty-eight. For his is the duty of proclaiming [the Veda] or teaching, and his responsibility for protection is greater than that of others. What offense is there for a common person who resembles an animal? Unlearned people, ignorant of virtues and faults, engage in improper acts. If even a learned man were to behave in the same way, alas, the world is lost, for there would be no third party to provide instruction. Thus it is said: "In this world, two are firm in their vows: the king and the Brāhmaṇa well-versed in scripture" (GDh 8.1). The former verse prescribes a higher fine for the king, while this one does so for the Brāhmaṇa. This is a rule regarding the mere principle of increase, not a rule prescribing the exact numbers as they are heard, because the fines for Brāhmaṇas are declared to be indefinite—"this or that"—and an option between them is not logical, as there is no cause for such a fixed arrangement (*vyavasthā*). An option is only possible when the alternatives are of equal force, since it is impossible to resort to another subject matter. For what king would abandon the "twice-born" status and take sixty-four? An option might be appropriate if the fine were for an invisible (transcendental) purpose; but it has already been stated that this is not for an invisible purpose. And Gautama says: "In the case of an offense by a learned man, the punishment must be more severe. Therefore, they declare that the rule is one of indefinite increase. Nor is an option based on qualities (*guṇa*) logical, since that is already provided for by the verse beginning with *naṣṭa* (MDh 8.232). Furthermore, the understanding here is of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) because it serves a purpose; and since that injunction finds its basis in the principle of increase, it is not capable of being construed as a literal alternative. (8.337–38)
Manu has declared that taking roots and fruits from trees, wood for the purpose of fire, and grass for the fodder of cows, does not constitute theft. (8.339)

*Vānaspatya* refers to trees, which are indeed *vanaspati*s; here the suffix is used in its own primary sense (*svārthe*). Taking bamboo shoots and the like for the purpose of eating constitutes non-stealing. Roots and fruits belong to the *vanaspati*s, while other things such as lotus stalks (*bisa*) and grain are different. In the list beginning with *sūtra* (MDh 8.326), a penalty is prescribed for taking roots and fruits for purposes other than eating. The statement regarding non-stealing applies to taking them for the sake of food—that is, for a limited quantity—even for one whose livelihood is not diminished, should he somehow become greedy, as seen in another *smṛti*; furthermore, there is a penalty for taking from what is not one's own property. Thus says Gautama: "One may take flowers as if they were one's own, and fruits from those [trees] that are not enclosed" (GDh 12.28). Wood for the sake of fire: if the fire of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) goes out because no *vanaspati* is nearby, taking wood for the purpose of maintaining it is faultless; or one should place fuel-sticks of *palāśa*. And if there is no abundance of *palāśa* in the village, how would this be possible? If they were to be taken [from elsewhere], there is no fault. And grass for cows: the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) here denotes purpose. Because of the mention of "for cows," if it were for making a mat (*prastāra*), there would indeed be a fault. As for those who wish to connect the word "for the sake of eating" (*grāsārtha*) with "cows," for them the expression "for cows" (*gobhyaḥ*) would be inappropriate; the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would be more suitable in that context. (MDh 8.339)
A Brahmin who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given, even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching, is just like a thief. (8.340)

This is an extended application (*atideśa*): A Brāhmaṇa who lives off thieves is to be punished like a thief—even by officiating at their sacrifices or teaching them. The word “even” (*api*) indicates other activities; by this, receiving gifts, accepting out of affection, and so forth are included. For Kṣatriyas and others, however, the case is different when they take the wealth of thieves through their own duties such as trade and the like. The specific mention of the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of removing the conceit: “I have indeed officiated at sacrifices while acquiring [wealth] according to dharma. One who takes what is not given—that is, seizes it—is a thief, an *adattādāyin*. If he should desire to obtain it (*lipseta*), meaning he wishes to acquire it even before the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been received, there shall be punishment for theft on account of that very connection. (8.340)
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose provisions are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be punished. (8.341)

The mention of the "twice-born" (dvija) is for the purpose of excluding the Śūdra. A traveler is one who does not reside in a single village; even among such travelers, he must be one whose means of subsistence are exhausted, meaning his provisions for the journey are spent. "Two stalks of sugarcane" and "two roots" are mentioned as illustrative examples; this also includes limited quantities of *harītakī*, mung beans, and other pulse-grains (*śamīdhānya*). Accordingly, another legal text (*smṛti*) states: "There is no prohibition regarding *śamī* pods, cucumbers, yokes, or fodder. "From another's field" means from a place belonging to another, even if it is enclosed by a fence. (8.341)
One who binds those already bound, one who releases those already bound, and one who seizes slaves, horses, and chariots, shall incur the guilt of a thief. (8.342)

Horses and other animals that have been freed from their chains and other bonds are kept in secluded places abounding in grass, barley, and the like. If, while the owner or the herdsman is asleep, someone should tether them with a halter or bind them with a bit and so forth, he should be punished like a thief, out of the suspicion that "surely this man intends to lead them away. However, there is no fault for one who binds [an animal] solely for the purpose of protecting it—such as one that has strayed from its owner’s house or arrived after being separated from its herd. The same penalty applies to cattle and other animals when they are bound by a rope around the neck or similar means. Furthermore, regarding those that are already tied with foot-chains and the like, the one who releases them is also liable; likewise, one who entices the keepers of ropes in secret and carries off bonded servants and the like, saying, "I will give you much; why do you serve him?"—in the case of carrying off persons of noble birth (*kulīna*), death is prescribed in the verse beginning with "of men" (MDh 8.323). By this, the rule for slaves is stated. Just as a person of noble birth was mentioned there, so too here, one must not carry them off by enticing them; whether by force or by theft. Regarding the phrase "stealer of horses and chariots": this refers to horses and chariots. In the verse "of large animals" (MDh 8.324), the horses belong to the king, whereas these [horses] belong to the common people. In the former case, the punishment is at the king's discretion, but here, death is fixed. Although there are many punishments for thieves, even so, according to another Smṛti:

"Men who capture thieves, those who carry off horses and elephants, and those who kill by force, one should impale upon a stake. (YDh 2.277). Here too, in a general sense, having begun with the words "by whatever [means]" (MDh 8.334), it concludes with "one should take that very same [means]" (MDh 8.334).
Others, however, consider "a chariot yoked with horses" to be a general term, because it serves as an illustration for [vehicles] such as those drawn by horses, oxen, and so forth.

In that regard, the punishment for the theft of horses alone and of a chariot must be considered. Since another Smṛti text prescribes the thief's penalty for the theft of horses alone, it is established that this applies even when they are yoked to a chariot. However, for those who consider "carrying away" (*haraṇa*) to mean taking [the animals] away after instigating them, the word "horse-chariot" (*aśvaratha*) indicates the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*), meaning the "maker of the chariot. And that [penalty] applies to all crafts. For the theft of artisans, the thief's penalty applies. As for the instigation of the horses, it occurs by showing them a mare. (8.342)
By carrying out the suppression of thieves according to this rule, a king shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death. (8.343)

By this aforementioned path, while suppressing thieves, one gains fame and the praise of all good people in this world for as long as life lasts; and after death, having passed away, one enjoys the unsurpassed happiness known as heaven. This is the conclusion of the section. (8.343)
A king who desires to attain the station of Indra and imperishable, undecaying glory should not overlook a man of violent deeds even for a moment. (8.344)

*Saḥas* means force; one who acts by means of that is a *sāhasika* (one who acts with violence). A person who, disregarding visible and invisible faults and relying solely on force, openly engages in acts such as theft, injury, or adultery which cause suffering to others, is a *sāhasika*. Thus it is said: "It may be *sahasam*" (MDh 8.332). *Sahasa* is not a distinct category of offense from theft and the like; rather, those very acts become *sāhasa* because they are committed by force. Even though acts such as arson or the tearing of clothes are already established as offenses because they consist of the destruction of property, the king should not overlook them nor delay even for a moment in their suppression. Once he has been caught, he must be punished immediately. Desiring to attain the station belonging to Indra—known as heaven—or else desiring his own royal position to be like that of Indra, characterized by immovability; for by punishing those deserving of punishment, subjects follow him through both his majesty and his favor. Thus it is said: "As rivers [flow] into the ocean" (MDh 8.175). "Inexhaustible fame" means undecaying. There are two subjects and two adjectives: "the station is undecaying" and "fame is inexhaustible. Alternatively, fame is qualified by both: *kṣaya* is a reduction in measure, while *vyaya* is total destruction without a trace. Neither of these applies to it. His fame does not become tarnished, nor is it ever interrupted. This is a praise consisting of a statement of fact. (8.344)
A man who commits violence through harsh speech, theft, or even by means of punishment, should be known as the worst among evildoers. (8.345)

This is a figurative statement intended to praise the method of punishment. One who is corrupt in speech is a "vāgduṣṭa," meaning a thief or robber; one who commits violence with a staff is a "daṇḍapāruṣyakṛt. Here, "staff" (daṇḍa) is used as a metaphor for any weapon. Compared to these three aforementioned evildoers, this person is the most excessive evildoer of all. (8.345)
But that king who tolerates one engaged in violence quickly goes to destruction and incurs hatred. (8.346)

This also is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). Regarding the man who stands by an act of violence and condones it: here the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has its primary sense. He who condones—that is, tolerates—meets with destruction and incurs hatred among the subjects, and he is overcome by those who hate him. (8.346)
A king should not, for the sake of a friend or from the acquisition of vast wealth, release those who act with violence and bring fear to all living beings. (8.347)

Therefore, it is said: one should not disregard a neighbor who is being entreated by a minister or others for some reason of affection; nor should one neglect him thinking, "He himself will give me very much wealth. Those who act with reckless violence bring fear to all living beings. This also is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). 8.347.
The twice-born may take up arms when their duty is obstructed, or during a upheaval of the twice-born and the social orders caused by the exigencies of time. (8.348)
One who kills in self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, or in order to protect a woman or a Brahmin, does not incur sin if he acts according to dharma. (8.349)

Because of the injunction, "He should carry a bamboo staff" (MDh 4.36), the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) are inferred to be permitted to carry weapons. Furthermore, a weapon provides an excess of strength to one who commits a violent act (*sāhasika*). Therefore, the taking up of a weapon—which would otherwise not be required—is prescribed out of the suspicion that one might become a perpetrator of violence: "Weapons may be taken up by the twice-born. At this point, the sentence is concluded. The remainder, however, is connected with the phrase "killing according to dharma"; thus, these are two distinct sentences.

As for those who maintain that one should take up arms only on these specific occasions and not otherwise, what recourse is there for one who has unexpectedly fallen into the hands of an assassin with a weapon drawn? For they do not expect him to wait for the taking up of a weapon. Now, if it is explained thus: "The sword is to be taken up when dharma is obstructed, during a calamity caused by time, when the king has transgressed, and when the established order has collapsed; but at other times, under a righteous reign, the king himself provides protection."

For a king cannot remain with his hands extended toward every individual. There are some wicked persons who even harass royal officers when they are engaged in their most heroic duties, yet they fear those who bear weapons; therefore, the constant carrying of arms is appropriate. Moreover, what need is there to mention merely seizing them, which serves as a mere source of intimidation?

"No," he says, "one who kills according to the law does not incur sin. This instruction extends even to the point of violence. As for what Āpastamba stated—"A Brāhmaṇa shall not take up a weapon even for the purpose of examination"—this is a prohibition against drawing it when the aforementioned cause is absent, not a prohibition against possessing it; for weapons are examined while unsheathed.

When there is an obstruction of Dharma—that is, when the destruction of sacrifices and other rites is carried out by certain individuals; when there is a confusion of castes (*varṇa*), meaning their lack of stability such as through the mixing of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*); and when it is caused by Time, such as the death of a king and so forth—in those circumstances, one may take up arms for the sake of protecting one's own wealth and family. Others, however, maintain that on this occasion one may do so even for the sake of others. And thus says Gautama: "And when there is violence against the weak, if one is capable of delivering them... (GDh 21.19).

It has been stated that taking up arms is for the purpose of averting the fear of the destruction of a sacrifice. He states another occasion: "And in self-defense. The prefix *pari-* signifies "on all sides. One who kills in accordance with dharma for the sake of protecting one's body, wife, wealth, or children does not incur sin. Furthermore, there is the "non-contradiction of agreements regarding sacrificial fees" (*dakṣiṇā-saṅgara*): if sacrificial fees intended for a sacrifice are seized by some, then one must fight on that account.

Others, however, connect it thus: "If, for the sake of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), an obstruction has arisen in battle, and the Dharma has not been practiced, that is called a 'contract for fees' (*dakṣiṇā-saṃgara*)."

The "overcoming" (*abhyavapatti*) of women and Brahmins refers to their humiliation (*paribhava*). Where virtuous women are approached by force by someone or killed, or likewise where Brahmins are killed by someone—there, the one who kills with a sword or other weapon incurs no fault. The meaning is that no transgression of the prohibition against violence has been committed. Since there is no prohibition [against such killing] and the possibility of acting according to one's own will (*kāmacāra*) arises, one must necessarily proceed to kill, reflecting upon the injunction of Gautama: "If capable, one should rescue [others] from the injury of the weak" (GDh 21.19). However, if there is a fear of a counter-attack, then one should remain indifferent, in accordance with the rule: "One should protect oneself from all sides" (GDh 9.34). 8.348–49.
One must fight without hesitation for the sake of self-preservation. He demonstrates this:
"Even if it be a teacher, or one who is young or old, or a learned Brahmin—if he comes as an assassin, one must certainly kill him without hesitation. (8.350)

One who is intent on destroying one’s body, wealth, wife, or sons is called an *ātatāyin* (an assailant). One may kill such a person without hesitation. The mention of the teacher (*guru*) and others is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), intended to show that even these persons should be killed, let alone others. However, even though they are *ātatāyins*, there is no killing [of them]; for by the rule, "And the teacher and the expounder" (MDh 4.162), the killing of even those who cause harm is prohibited. The connection "the teacher who is an *ātatāyin*" is possible; if that were the case, this would be a qualification of the *ātatāyin*. Consequently, how could there be a prohibition against an *ātatāyin* distinct from the teacher and others? For there is no other scriptural statement to that effect.

Now, as for the argument that this other statement, "There is no fault in killing an *ātatāyin*," (MDh 8.351) is a general authorization, that too is not correct; because no injunction (*vidhi*) is heard therein, and since it functions as an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the preceding [text], it refers only to the subject matter at hand.

In this regard, however, you [the opponents] say: "Even if the injunction is simply 'one who is an *ātatāyin*,' and the remainder is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), nevertheless there is permission for the killing of teachers and others; because being a wrongdoer (*apakārī*) is one thing, while being an *ātatāyin* is another. For one who inflicts some kind of injury but not with his entire body and so forth is a wrongdoer, whereas another is an *ātatāyin*. And thus it is recited: 'One with a raised sword, one with poison or fire, one with a hand raised to cast a curse, one who kills by means of the *Atharvaveda*, a slanderer, and also one who acts against the king.'"

"One who violates his wife and one who is intent on seeking out one's weaknesses—one should recognize all such persons as *ātatāyin*s (assassins). Regarding this, some say: "Because of the word 'approaching' (*āyāntam*), one who is rushing forward with a weapon to kill, or wishing to seize one's wife, must be killed; however, once the offense has been committed, one should remain indifferent, thinking, 'What else will he do?'"

That is incorrect, because [the author] will state later: "Whether openly or secretly" (MDh 8.351). For he intends these two cases—those who are about to act and those who have already acted—to be equal. Therefore, the phrase "one who is coming" is a restatement meaning: one who has come to act, or one who has departed after having acted. Furthermore, such a person is slain on account of being an *ātatāyin* (an assassin or one intent on immediate violence). And the status of being an *ātatāyin* does not depend on the fact that he has already completed the act. Nor is his killing intended solely for the protection of oneself; this has been stated by the rule: "and in the protection of oneself" (MDh 8.349). (8.350)
There is no fault whatsoever for the slayer in killing an assassin, whether done openly or in secret; fury recoils upon that fury. (8.351)

"No one at all" means: there is neither demerit (*adharma*), nor punishment, nor penance. "Publicly" means in the presence of people; "secretly" means by administering poison or by any other such means. *Manyu* is the deity presiding over anger; he encounters that *manyu*. Herein, there is no relationship of killer and killed. This is a figurative statement (*arthavāda*) meaning that when the object of two men is the wrath of an assassin (*ātatāyin*), the other is killed. Just as one desiring to receive a gift might say, "Who shall give to me? I am not the receiver, nor are you the giver; therefore, how can the fault of receiving a gift affect me? so it is here as well. No specific punishment for this perpetrator of violence is mentioned here; it should be understood from the section on physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*). However, in this case, the penalty is greater, since it has been stated: "He should be known as the worst among evildoers" (MDh 8.345). 8.351.
The king, having branded those men who have committed an assault on another's wife with punishments that cause terror, shall banish them. 8.352.

The word *dāra* (wife) applies to a woman who has been consecrated through marriage. "Another" (*para*) means someone other than oneself. "Touching" (*abhimarśa*) refers to sexual enjoyment, beginning from embracing; embracing is the coming together of two persons. The "commencement" (*pravṛtti*) of the pleasure born of enjoyment is its initiation—the incitement by sending a female messenger and so forth for the purpose of engaging in it. Furthermore, they declare that "seizing" (*saṃgrahaṇa*) is touching. Therefore, the meaning is this: having recognized a man intent on approaching the wife of another, one should brand him with sharp-pointed weapons such as spears or tridents that cause terror, and then banish him by means of cutting off his nose and so forth. Since a specific punishment has been stated here in every case, this is not a general punishment, but rather applies to repeated practice. This, however, is appropriate: for one who does not obtain [his desire], there is a combination of banishment and a monetary fine because of the difference in the nature of the offense. We shall demonstrate this accordingly. (8.352)
For from that arises the confusion of castes among the world, by which unrighteousness, which destroys the very root, leads to total destruction. (8.353)

*Samutthāna* means origin. From that—namely, from approaching another’s wife—*saṃkara* (intermixture of castes), which takes the form of intermediate castes, is born. By the birth of such [offspring], *adharma* seizes the rain that has fallen from heaven for the sake of the root-world; for when *dharma* exists, it is said: “From the sun, rain is produced” (MDh 3.66). And when *saṃkara* exists, there is neither the *Kārīrī* sacrifice nor the giving of gifts to a worthy recipient. Thus, due to the absence of gifts, sacrifices, and oblations—which are the causes for the production of crops—it becomes capable of destroying the entire world. Therefore, one should banish those who approach another’s wife, protecting the rain which is the root of the production of crops and so forth, lest there be an intermixture of castes, the root of *adharma*. (8.353)
A man who engages in private conversation with another's wife, having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement. (8.354)

"Conversation" (*saṃbhāṣa*) means talking; engaging in such talk—meaning carrying on a conversation—with one who has previously been accused or charged with offenses such as adultery, such as soliciting her woman, or who is fickle, having been seen committing such an offense against another or whose guilt is suspected; or, according to some, one with whom conversation is forbidden in private, such as at a well or similar places—even if conversing with another's wife for a specific reason, he shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; that is to say, he must be made to pay it. (8.354)
But he who, having not been previously accused, speaks out for a valid reason, shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part. (8.355)
This is a counter-example to the preceding rule: even if one has not been accused, by conversing with or mixing with [a sinner] without cause, one incurs the same penalty as before. (8.355)
He who addresses another's wife at a sacred bathing place, in a wilderness, or even in a forest, or at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery. (8.356)

Since the phrase "another's wife" (*parasya patnyā*) was already established [in MDh 8.354], the explicit mention of "another's woman" (*parastrī*) here is for the purpose of not excluding the mother, sister, the teacher’s wife, and so forth; for although they too have a connection with another, they are not designated as "another's wife."

A *tīrtha* is said to be a path by which people descend to fetch water from rivers, ponds, and the like; for such a place is generally secluded, and one does not remain there merely for the purpose of water. In this context, a *tīrtha* is conceived as a meeting place where one must certainly go. [The author thinks: "If I were to stay here, I would not be suspected, as people would think, 'He is waiting either because he is seeking water or because he is performing his daily purification rites during the day. In another location, however, there might be suspicion: 'Why is he waiting here? Therefore, there is a prohibition against [meeting] at a *tīrtha*. An *araṇya* (forest) is a region devoid of people beyond the village, thick with shrubs, trees, creepers, and the like. A *vana* (wood) is a continuous stretch of trees. The *saṃbheda* (confluence) of rivers is their meeting point; that too is a meeting place. He would incur the charge of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse). *Saṃgrahaṇa* consists in the desire for another's wife. Thus, it is implied that whatever punishment applies there shall apply to him. This prohibition holds even for one who has not been accused, even if there is a cause [for suspicion]. As for what Āpastamba stated—"One should not pass by a woman without speaking"—that refers to cases where other people are present who know this law, and where it is in public; in such a case, one should perform a salutation without delay, saying, "Sister! Salutations to you," and so forth. (8.356)
Acts of service, playful dalliance, touching her ornaments and garments, and even sitting upon the same bed—all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery). 8.357.

To provide assistance to one who is not related by any kinship through the giving of garments, garlands, and the like; likewise, through food, drink, and so forth; "play" means joking or using indirect speech and the like; "touching" refers to ornaments and clothes—namely, necklaces, bracelets, and so on, which have come into contact with her body; having recognized them as hers, one touches them even when they are held by another, without any other purpose; and sitting together on the same bed, even though their limbs do not touch—each of these acts carries the same punishment. (8.357)

If one touches a woman in an improper place, or if, being touched by her, he consents to it—with mutual agreement, all such acts are recorded in the law as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct). || 8.358 ||

However, there is no fault in the case of *adeśasparśa* (contact in a non-designated place), where acts such as coming and going are accomplished even without that physical contact. There is likewise no fault in a crowd of many people. Furthermore, a part of the body is also considered a "place. In that regard, there is no fault in touching an object being held by the hand or shoulder when one is setting it down; however, there is a fault regarding the lips, chin, breasts, and so forth. Or, if she is pressed by the touch of her breasts and the like, yet endures it and does not forbid him by saying, "Do not do this," and so on—provided this occurs with mutual consent and intentionally—there is no fault in this act. But this is not the case at the beginning of the ritual action (*karmādau*). If a woman, while stumbling, clings to a man’s neck, or a man clings to a woman between her breasts, during the process of taking up an object grasped by her hand—just as one who intends to fall on dry ground might instead fall into mud—neither of them would be at fault. (8.358)
A non-Brahmin who commits adultery deserves a punishment ending in death;
for the wives of all four castes must always be protected with the utmost care. (8.359)

The nature of sexual intercourse (*saṃgraha*) has been explained. The punishment (*daṇḍa*) is now stated here. A non-Brāhmaṇa—such as a Kṣatriya or others—when he has committed sexual intercourse, deserves a punishment ending in death, that is, resulting in the loss of life, regardless of the distinction between high and low castes among the four *varṇas*.
But how can there be an equal punishment for one who has had intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman and a Śūdra woman?

Here he states the meaning of the nature of the reason (*hetu*): "Wives must always be protected most carefully. A king must protect the wives of anyone whatsoever more than their wealth or bodies. For if there is an equal degree of intermixture (*saṅkara*), even for a Śūdra, it results in the destruction of the family. This is what is meant: this matter, which is based on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), must be stated as the reason here; that has now been stated.

Regarding this, earlier commentators have explained: "This previously mentioned punishment does not apply to every instance of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse). Rather, it applies to the primary form of *gamana* (coitus), which consists of a specific pleasure produced by a specific kind of touch. For how else could saluting at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and coitus be subject to the same punishment? Therefore, a non-Brāhmaṇa—specifically a Śūdra—is liable to the loss of life for approaching a twice-born woman, and no one else. Indeed, it is not right to equate what is unequal. Consequently, in the cases of *saṃgrahaṇa* mentioned above, the punishment must be determined with regard to the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*) and other factors. Only where it is certain that this preliminary action, such as offering assistance, was intended solely for the purpose of coitus, is the primary punishment appropriate; for in such a case there is no inequality. And this is observed to be the case in both instances."
Thus it has been said: "If this punishment applies here to the primary form of sexual intercourse (*saṃgrahaṇa*), what will it do?

For there is no other such thing as "primary sexual intercourse. Indeed, its worldly referent is not determined, such that one could say it is applied specifically to acts like assisting another's wife. And as for that which you consider the "primary" sexual intercourse, there is a heavy punishment for it; for approaching another's wife is prohibited and must be accounted for according to the scriptures. If [it is argued]: "But..."
Know that there is a prohibition even regarding acts of assistance and the like.
If it is argued that, just as with the prohibition, penance would likewise necessarily apply in equal measure, [we reply:]...

What undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*) is this? However, it would follow [only] when that [act] is denoted by the term "sexual intercourse" (*saṃgrahaṇa*). For it is only when semen has been emitted that there is the designation of "approaching" (*gamana*) and so forth. Wherever such a punishment exists, there a corresponding suffering is incurred. Therefore, in this contrary case, since the term [“sexual intercourse”] denotes the cause of semen emission, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should be applied to acts such as offering assistance and the like. If, however, there were only a minor punishment for conversation and so forth, people would engage in them. Consequently, those whose passion is inflamed by another who overcomes them through conversation with another’s wife and so on—being dragged along by the arrows of Love (*smara*) and indifferent to their bodies—would not take account of royal punishment. But if they are apprehended at the very first engagement, while the passion is still not firmly established, it is possible to ward it off. Therefore, a heavy punishment is appropriate precisely for one who attempts to seduce another’s wife.

In this context, however, because of the mention of the "end" (*anta*), there must be another punishment that serves as the beginning. For they do not become speakers of untruth. That which has life as its end is "life-ending"; it should be inflicted until it falls upon the vital breaths. By this, the seizure of all property, the cutting off of limbs, and so forth, are also implied. Furthermore, the status of being a "punishment" is known for each individual case elsewhere; one is not punished for a collection [of offenses]. Thus, when many punishments are prescribed, that which applies to a non-Brāhmaṇa for sexual intercourse with a woman of the twice-born caste is the greatest. Therefore, this interpretation is indeed appropriate, and not applicable everywhere. In that regard, for one who has sexual intercourse with women of good family who are unwilling and have husbands, the penalty is the taking of life; the same applies even to those of low birth. (8.359)
Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice, and artisans may converse with women without being forbidden. (8.360)

Beggars who live on alms may engage in conversation consisting of requests for alms without being forbidden, provided they have not been prohibited by their master; or rather, they should not be prevented at all. Bards and panegyrists, as well as those consecrated for a sacrifice when speaking for the purpose of receiving wages, and artisans such as cooks and the like—these should not be barred even at sacred bathing places and similar locations. (8.360)
One who has been forbidden should not engage in conversation with the wives of others; but he who converses despite being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa. (8.361)
Some believe that this penalty applies to those such as mendicants who have been forbidden from conversing;

however, that is incorrect, for it has already been stated that they are not to be forbidden at all. Furthermore, why would there be a fine of one *suvarṇa* for mendicants? Therefore, anyone who, though publicly unaccused, has somehow been prohibited by his master and yet continues to act [with him], shall be fined one *suvarṇa*. (8.361)
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers, nor to those who live off their own wives;
for they entice women and keep them hidden away. (8.362)

The prohibition against conversation and the prohibition against performing services for prostitutes (*cāraṇa*) should not apply here. *Cāraṇas* are actors, singers, and others who perform spectacles. Likewise, there are those who live off their own wives—those who subsist on the wives of such performers. Alternatively, as it is said, "This [wife] is indeed half of one's self" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 5.2.1.10), there are those who live off that [half-self] by tolerating paramours; they are *cāraṇas* because they "join together" (*sajjayanti*), that is, they cause union with another man. They are "hidden," meaning they remain concealed and do not stand in the marketplace. Because they wear the dress of householders, they are distinguished from well-known courtesans. They "cause to circulate" (*cārayanti*) sexual intercourse; they attract men through the play of eyes and eyebrows, jesting, and so forth. "Joining" (*sajjana*) means consenting to that, and "causing to circulate" (*cāraṇa*) is the act of sexual union itself. Alternatively, they "join" (*sajjayanti*) their own women, and they "cause others to circulate" (*cārayanti*) with women, meaning they cause their own women to practice the profession of courtesans or procuresses. (8.362)
But he who engages in conversation with such women, or with female slaves who eat only once a day, or with female ascetics in secret, shall be made to pay a small fine. (8.363)

If he converses in secret, in private, or in a secluded place with courtesans, he shall be fined a very small amount of gold—such as one-thirtieth part or similar—taking into account his caste and social standing; for in their case, the status of a courtesan is not complete, since they consort with men only when permitted by their husbands. In such matters, dealings must be conducted through a female messenger to ascertain the husband's consent, and not directly with them, because they lack independence. However, conversation during public performances—such as when they are dancing or singing and there is an occasion to observe the gestures, rhythm, and so forth—is not prohibited, provided it takes the form of questions such as "How is this? and the like.

Female servants (*preṣyā*) and slave-girls (*dāsyaḥ*), brought from the seven sources of slavery, belong to one [master]; they have a single devotion and are confined by one. In that regard, there is even a slight trace of punishment. But as for this word "slave-girl" (*dāsī*): is it a relative term such that she is the slave of whoever is her master, or is it based on her occupation, like the words "cook" (*sūpakāra*) and so forth?

In this case, the first position alone holds, because the inclusion of the qualification [“of one’s own”] would be redundant. A woman who belongs to someone as a servant or a courtesan, and who associates with others—whether she is a royal slave or a common slave—is restrained [from such conduct]. If she is not kept [as a concubine], there is no offense in the act of sexual intercourse (*saṃgrahaṇa*). If she is kept, the punishment for that has been stated by this [rule]. We shall explain this in detail in the section on the division of inheritance. Those who have entered religious orders (*pravrajitāḥ*) are unprotected, such as Śīlamitra and others; for they, like libertines, conceal their true nature under the guise of their [religious] marks. (8.363)
He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution;
but a man who violates one who is willing, being equal to her in status, shall not suffer death. (8.364)

This is incidental. "Equal" means of the same class. He who should defile an unwilling maiden—that is, deprive her of her virginity through sexual intercourse with a male—must be killed immediately on that very day, without delay. There is no defilement in the case of a willing woman; how, then, could there be the attainment of the death penalty? We shall explain what will follow in this regard. Although only "equal punishment" is heard here, even regarding the execution, when a consideration of caste is necessarily required, the rule is restricted by proximity. (8.364)
One should not cause a maiden who is associating with a superior man to pay anything at all;
however, if she is serving an inferior man, one should keep her confined in the house.

One should not punish in any way a woman who has engaged in sexual intercourse with a man superior to her father’s family in even one of the qualities of birth, wealth, character, or learning. Since a maiden lacks independence, this prohibition is established against the punishment that would otherwise fall upon her guardians, such as her father and others. If she consorts with a base man—one inferior in birth and other qualities—and persists in her desire for sexual union, she should be restrained, deprived of play and diversions, and placed under the supervision of chamberlains, or kept within her father’s house itself, until her lust has ceased. If, however, her particular passion for a man of low birth has been extinguished, then she shall remain restrained until her very last breath. (8.365)
But a man of lower caste who has intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves death;
one who has intercourse with a woman of equal caste should pay a fine, provided her father desires it. (8.366)

It has been stated that for the violation of an unwilling maiden—excluding the case of a Brāhmaṇa—the punishment is death without distinction for those of lower or higher status. However, regarding the violation of a willing maiden, they say this: if a man of very low status violates a woman of superior status in terms of beauty, youth, or caste, he is to be put to death even if there is not great disparity in their qualities. But if he approaches a willing woman of equal status, he should pay her father a bride-price (*śulka*) as in the *Āsura* form of marriage. If the father does not wish to accept it, then he must pay an equivalent fine to the king.
But surely, this is a *gāndharva* marriage, defined as "union through mutual desire" (MDh 3.32); in that case, punishment is not appropriate.

It has been said that in the *gāndharva* form there is no punishment; for this very reason, this is not the duty of a virtuous wife (*satī-dharma*), nor is it a valid marriage, due to the absence of the consecration by fire (*agni-saṃskāra*). As for the statement by Vyāsa in the *Śākuntala*, "without mantras, without fire," that was done by Duṣyanta precisely because he was tormented by desire. Moreover, a mere union based on mutual consent is not marriage. There are eight types of marriages according to the different means of formal acceptance (*svīkaraṇa-upāya*), but not because there are different kinds of marriage. In such cases, the formal selection of the groom (*varaṇa*) must nevertheless be performed again.

Alternatively, the *gāndharva* form [of marriage] occurs after the appearance of menses; prior to the menses, there is either a bride-price (*śulka*) or a fine. Now, what is the course of action regarding the maiden? She should be given back to that very same man. If her desire has ceased, she may, at will, marry elsewhere. Even in this case, the taking of a bride-price exists indeed as a compensation for a single act of sexual enjoyment. If the groom’s desire has ceased, he must be made to accept her by force. (8.366)
