But the man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force, his two fingers shall be immediately cut off, and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas]. (8.367)

Even if the maiden is willing, if her father or other guardians are present, he may—by means of arrogance and force, overcoming them against their will and thinking, "Who is capable of doing anything to me?"—act toward the maiden based solely on her affection; he may violate, alter, or defile her. The root *kṛ* has many meanings here. Her fingers should be quickly cut off, half-finger-breadth at a time, or he should be fined six hundred [paṇas].
Others, however, hold that this is a summary of the meaning of the death penalty found in the verse, "He who would defile a maiden against her will" (MDh 8.364).
The meaning of "to be killed" extends from being beaten up to being put to death. In this regard, one who defiles a woman of low caste is not killed, but rather his finger shall be cut off. (8.367)
One who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the same punishment as one who cuts off her finger;
rather, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas to prevent a recurrence of such conduct. (8.368)

The phrase "with her consent" (*sakāmām*) is a restatement, as the preceding rule also pertains to cases involving a willing woman. Regarding the act committed by force (*abhiṣahya*), the previous punishment [of two hundred panas] applies; however, if done secretly, the penalty is like that for theft—two hundred panas—excluding the amputation of the fingers. Now, suppose there is a maiden who feels affection for a certain man, and while being united with him, she loses her virginity; this punishment applies to the one who, knowing her to be "willing," causes her to become defiled. Alternatively, here "defilement" (*dūṣaṇa*) may refer merely to the touch of the hand. The touching of the hand of a maiden who is to be sought in marriage is intended so that others, perceiving "she has been touched by me," will not seek her out, thinking her to be already attached to another. (MDh 8.368)
If a maiden should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod. (8.369)

If a maiden, out of childishness or out of aversion to [another] form and so forth, should ruin another maiden, she shall be made to pay two hundred [paṇas]; and the bride-price (śulka) shall be tripled. What, then, is the measure of the bride-price?
It depends on the particular beauty of form and such among these [maidens], and it depends on her good fortune.
*Śiphā* refers to blows with a rope or a creeper. (8.369)
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head, or else the cutting off of two fingers, and likewise being led away on a donkey. (8.370)

When a woman destroys the female characteristics of virgins, her punishment is shaving the head—that is, the cutting off of the hair—or the amputation of a finger; if the latter option is chosen, she must be led away on a donkey. Depending on the distinctions of caste and so forth among the virgins, and the distinctions of the offender to be punished, some authorities desire this punishment for women of the three higher castes according to the sequence starting with Brahmin women, and they prescribe various marks [on their foreheads]. These should be disregarded due to a lack of authoritative proof. (8.370)
But that woman who, arrogant on account of her kinsmen or her own virtues, should transgress against her husband,
the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public place crowded with many people.

*Laṅghana* is going elsewhere after transgressing against one’s husband. If a woman does this out of pride—thinking, "I have many kinsmen who are powerful and wealthy," or "I possess the excellence of feminine qualities such as beauty and good fortune; what is the use of this [husband's] character and appearance?"—if she acts with such pride, he shall have her devoured by dogs until she dies. *Saṃsthāna* means a place; a location where many people are gathered, such as a crossroads and the like. (8.371)
They should burn the sinful man on a heated iron bed;
they should pile wood upon it, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire. (8.372)

That man who is the paramour of the wife shall be burned on a red-hot iron bed made like fire; and while he lies there upon the bed, the executioners shall pile wood over him and cast it on top, until he dies from the blows of the wood, the flames of the fire, and the heat of the bed. 8.372.
For a wicked man who has been accused for a full year, the fine shall be doubled;
likewise, for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī* woman, the fine is exactly that much.

"Accused" (*abhiśasta*) means one who is proclaimed as a perpetrator of that [crime]. He who is apprehended with a woman is "accused" and punished. If, after having been released for a year, he is again apprehended with that same woman once the year has passed, then for him—having been accused once and becoming an offender again after a year has elapsed—the punishment is double.
This is how the compound *saṃvatsarābhiśastasya* is to be construed in some way.

"In cohabitation with a *vrātyā*, it is exactly the same. To what extent? "As much as for a corrupt woman (*duṣṭā*). We say: "No. For even there, the punishment is of various kinds—highest, lowest, or middling. In that case, it is not known which one applies here. What then? "In cohabitation with a *caṇḍālī*, it is exactly the same as with a *vrātyā*," according to the rule: "But [the fine for] stealing from an outcaste is one thousand [paṇas]" (MDh 8.385). A *vrāta* is a multitude, a crowd, or a group; she who moves about with such a group is a harlot (*puṃścalī*)—this is how the term must somehow be understood. Alternatively, let it be that she who deserves a *vrāta* is a *vrātyā*; the suffix *-ya-* is added in the sense of "deserving" (Pāṇini 5.1.66). And who deserves a *vrāta*? A harlot, who is to be enjoyed by many men, for she indeed deserves a multitude of men (*puruṣavrāta*). Or else, those who belong to a multitude of men as their masters—the female slaves of a village—are *vrātyās*. As for those who consider a girl who has not been married to be a *vrātyā*, in their view the primary meaning of the word is not maintained. For this word *vrātya* is used by the authors of the *Smṛtis* for those who have fallen away from the *Sāvitrī* initiation. And that [falling away] is not possible for women. If it is argued that for women, initiation (*upanayana*) consists in marriage because of the scriptural statement regarding its attainment, and thus a woman who lacks it is a *vrātyā* like a man who lacks it, then the term is figurative (*gauṇa*), not primary (*mukhya*). Even if the word "initiation" is applied to marriage—which is not actually initiation—nevertheless, when it is said "one who lacks initiation is a *vrātyā*," it is not understood to mean "one who lacks marriage. Just as when it is said, "This country is full of lions," the fact that the word "lion" is applied to a boy does not imply that the country is not a country. If you argue that the primary meaning exists elsewhere and is impossible here, we reply: a figurative understanding is not based merely on impossibility; rather, it disregards another relationship. The word "initiation" might be figurative for marriage, but what is the reason for the word *vrātyā* being figurative? Even if it is figurative, the claim that it is based on the absence of marriage is difficult to establish. Regarding the offspring of a *vrātyā* (*vrātyajā*): just as a crow born from a crow is a crow, or a hawk born from a hawk is a hawk, she is suspected of being a *vrātyā*. For in those cases, the transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*) is understood through the proximity of many relationships. However, the wife of a *vrātya* (*vrātyabhāryā*), despite the existence of a relationship, cannot be designated by the word *vrātyā*. For the designation "so-and-so's wife" (*puṃyogāt ākhyāyām*) would apply only if there were a direct connection such as "this is his [son]," and in that case, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would be used to express the distinction. Therefore, if the word *vrātyā* is to be taken figuratively, one should understand her to be born of such a person. But if it is taken in its literal sense—"she who deserves a *vrāta*"—then a woman who has failed in marriage is neither the primary nor the figurative meaning. Furthermore, there is no fixed time for the marriage of women such that they would become *vrātyās* by failing at that specific time. Even as for the rule that they should be married before puberty, that refers to the *svayaṃvara* (self-choice); otherwise, even after that, she may remain in her father's house as long as she desires, until death, provided she has not been permitted [to marry] by him. (MDh 8.373)

A Śūdra who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the twice-born castes—whether she be protected or unprotected—is deprived of a limb if she was unprotected, and of his entire property if she was protected. (8.374)

A Śūdra down to a Caṇḍāla, or one of the twice-born castes having sexual intercourse with the protected women of the twice-born castes while they are being guarded by their husbands or others, shall be punished according to the rule. If it is asked what the punishment is: "If he approaches an unprotected woman, he is deprived of a limb and of his entire property. He is the possessor of both the limb and the entire property. By whom is he deprived? Because the subject under discussion is those two [the husband and the guardian], and because no other person is specified, and because no distinction is made, it is the offender himself who is deprived of the limb. If he approaches a protected woman, he is deprived of everything; not merely of one limb, but even of his whole body. By the mention of "deprivation," the cutting off of limbs, the confiscation of all property, and death are prescribed. The meaning is that "his deprivation must be carried out. And so says Gautama: "In the case of approaching an Āryan woman, the cutting off of the organ and the confiscation of all property; if she is protected... (GDh 12.2–3). [8.374]
A Vaiśya shall be punished with the forfeiture of all his property after being imprisoned for one year;
a Kṣatriya shall be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.

For a Vaiśya, the punishment of forfeiture of all property has been prescribed. However, here, due to association, even though he is a twice-born (dvijāti), this punishment does not apply to a Vaiśya upon approaching a woman of his own caste; rather, it applies only to a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya. Thus, for a Kṣatriya approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman, the punishment is one thousand [paṇas] and shaving with urine. In place of water, donkey’s urine should be used. Others explain: since no other [caste] is mentioned, the increase in punishment through confinement for one year applies only to one of the same caste. If he keeps her confined for a year, then this punishment follows.

However, the first explanation alone is logical. Nor should it be asked how there can be equal punishment for those who are equal, inferior, or superior; for it has been stated: "The wives of all social classes must always be protected most carefully" (MDh 8.359). || 8.375 ||
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman,
the king should fine the Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and the Kṣatriya one thousand.

The unprotected woman has already been explained; she is one who has fallen from her virtue and is without a protector. For approaching her, one should impose a fine of five hundred [paṇas] upon the Vaiśya. The root *kṛ* (to do) functions here, by virtue of the context, in the sense of punishing; thus, the meaning is "one should punish. The term *pañcaśataḥ* means "that which consists of five hundred," a Bahuvrīhi compound with a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*). It should be carried out in such a way that he comes to possess five hundred. Does this mean that whatever is in excess of that must be confiscated from him? We say: no. For if that were the case, no punishment would be prescribed for one whose wealth consists of exactly five hundred or less.

What, then, is the meaning of the phrase "one should impose five hundred"? Because the context concerns punishment, it means one should impose a fine consisting of five hundred. Likewise, regarding the phrase "a Kṣatriya possessing a thousand": he possesses a thousand as his fine, not wealth in his house. This should be explained according to [the rule] "one who has a limb or his entire property" (MDh 8.374): it must be done in such a way that his punishment consists of either a limb or his entire property. A Kṣatriya, being authorized for protection, protects; yet he himself commits an offense against that very duty. (8.376)
But both of them, having violated a protected Brahmin woman, should be punished like Śūdras or burned in a fire of straw. (8.377)

Those same Kṣatriya and Vaiśya [who have] violated a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman—that is, having had sexual intercourse with her—are to be punished like Śūdras, provided they were engaged in the act of intercourse at the time; for it is said, "A guarded woman is lost to everyone. Alternatively, they may be burned by a fire of straw (*kaṭāgni*). The word "or" (*vā*) is used to indicate an alternative regarding the manner of execution, not an alternative regarding the execution itself; for no punishment other than death is prescribed for a Śūdra who violates a guarded woman. (8.377)
A Brahmin who approaches a guarded Brahmin woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]; he who has sexual intercourse with a willing woman shall be fined five hundred. (8.378)

If a guarded woman, even one of fallen character, is protected by her father, brother, or kinsmen, a Brāhmaṇa who approaches her by force shall be made to pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas]. If she is both guarded and of virtuous character, there shall be banishment and branding as an additional penalty. Now, although the word "guarded" (*guptā*) may also refer to one who is virtuous, nevertheless, the Brāhmaṇa is released from liability beyond the mere fine of one thousand; for branding and banishment are applied in all cases of violating another's wife. (8.378)
Shaving the head is prescribed as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the other castes, the punishment shall be one that ends in death. (8.379)

Where the execution of Kṣatriyas and others is prescribed, there the shaving of the head (*mauṇḍya*) applies to a Brāhmaṇa. For example, as in: "A non-Brāhmaṇa deserves a punishment ending in death for adultery" (MDh 8.359), and likewise: "One should burn a man [guilty of violating a Guru’s bed]" (MDh 8.372). The term *prāṇāntaka* means that which goes to the end of life, or that which causes the end of life. The suffix *ṇvul* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.101 (*anyeṣv api dṛśyate*). Others, however, read the variant *prāṇāntika*. It is derived from *prāṇānta* with the suffix *ṭhañ*, according to the rule for words beginning with *adhyātma* (Pāṇini 4.3.60), meaning "that which exists at the end of life."

For others—that is, for the castes other than Brāhmaṇas, such as Kṣatriyas and so forth—the [penalty] is heard to be ending only in death, preceded by execution and the like. Immediately after that, this is stated. They consider that the shaving of the head (*mauṇḍya*) being mentioned is prescribed as a fine of one thousand [paṇas] as a subsidiary to that [death penalty]. Otherwise, since the death penalty has been prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, what occasion would there be for a Brāhmaṇa such that it is stated thus: "the shaving of the head ending in death"? If it is argued that this follows from the general rule "one should burn the man" (MDh 8.372), then it should apply to that very case; for in that way, its applicability to that specific subject would be clearly understood. (8.379)
One must never kill a Brahmin, even if he is established in every kind of sin; one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and unhurt. (8.380)

Regarding the phrase "in all sins," this rule of procedure applies not only to the offense of sexual intercourse with a woman of the same caste, but also to other transgressions. The word "api" (even) implies that even for one who has committed every possible sin, a Brāhmaṇa must never, at any time, be killed. What, then, should be done for that sinner? One should banish this Brāhmaṇa from the kingdom or the territory; that is, one should expel him. He should be made "possessed of his entire wealth," meaning accompanied by all his property, and "unwounded," meaning with his body intact. Even his wealth must not be confiscated. How, then, is the Brāhmaṇa to be punished?
Some say that when exile is being imposed, the provision of "with property" prohibits the imposition of a monetary fine.
Others, however, believe that he is to be exiled after having been deprived of his entire wealth and stripped of all his possessions. (8.380)
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even conceive of his execution in his mind. (8.381)

This is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to what precedes. There is no other unrighteousness (*adharma*) greater than the killing of a Brahmin that results in such suffering. The ablative case is used by supplying the word "other" (*anya*). For that reason, a king should not—even in his mind—desire the execution or the mutilation of this Brahmin’s limbs. (8.381)
If a Vaiśya should approach a protected Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya a protected Vaiśya woman, both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman. (8.382)

Regarding sexual intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman, [Manu Smṛti 8.376 states]: "One should fine a Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas], and a Kṣatriya one thousand. In that case, the fine for the Vaiśya is five hundred. It is appropriate that the punishment for him be so great, since he alone is the one who protects and yet he himself causes the destruction. 8.382.
A Brāhmaṇa, however, committing adultery with guarded women of those [castes], shall be made to pay a fine of one thousand;
for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya committing it with a Śūdra woman, the punishment shall indeed be one thousand.

A Brāhmaṇa who has intercourse with a concealed Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman shall be fined one thousand; this applies even when the punishment of banishment and branding remains in force. For intercourse with a Śūdra woman, the fine for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya is one *sāhasra*. The term *sāhasra* means "one thousand" (derived from *sahasra* with the suffix *aṇ* in its own sense). Alternatively, *sāhasra* refers to that which possesses a thousand, meaning the fine is one thousand; here the suffix *aṇ* has a possessive sense (*matvarthīya*). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.383)
If a Kṣatriya has sexual intercourse with an unprotected Vaiśya woman, the fine shall be five hundred;
however, the Kṣatriya shall undergo tonsure with urine, or else pay a fine. (8.384)

If a Vaiśya has intercourse with an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, his fine shall be five hundred [paṇas]. For a Kṣatriya who does the same, the penalty is the same; or he shall undergo the shaving of his head by means of donkey urine. This same punishment for both applies in the case of approaching a Vaiśya woman. (8.384)

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred; but if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyaja), he shall be fined one thousand.

In the case of a Brāhmaṇa having intercourse with an unprotected woman of the Kṣatriya class or others, there is punishment for both. An *antyaja* refers to a Caṇḍāla, Śvapaca, and so forth; in that case, the fine is one thousand [paṇas]. Herein is the summary of the punishment of one thousand *praṇas*: for a Brāhmaṇa’s illicit approach to a protected woman of any of the four castes, the fine is one thousand; in the case of the wives of a *śrotriya*, there is banishment and branding; in other cases, there is merely banishment. This is prescribed specifically because of the great severity of the penance required for the wives of a *śrotriya*. For approaching an unprotected woman, the fine is five hundred, along with banishment and branding. Even though an unprotected woman may be designated as another's wife when she has undergone the sacrament of marriage, nevertheless, being a wanton woman who has transgressed her husband’s authority, the punishment for a non-Brāhmaṇa for forcibly approaching a protected woman is the death penalty. In the case of approaching a willing woman, the fine is one thousand, along with banishment and branding. Regarding approaching a protected woman, [Manu says]: "One should impose a fine of five hundred on a Vaiśya and one thousand on a Kṣatriya" (MDh 8.376). 8.385.
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil, and no perpetrator of violence or one who strikes with impunity, shares in the world of Śakra.

That king in whose city, district, or kingdom there is no thief or robber attains the world and station of Śakra, the Lord; he reaches heaven. "One who does not go to another's wife"—that is, one who does not approach the wife or concubine of another, or a remarried woman (punarbhū). The mention of the word "woman" (*strī*) is for the purpose of prohibiting even those who are not wives and are unrelated. A "speaker of evil words" is one who utters the three kinds of abuse. A "violent person" has already been described. One who strikes with a staff is a perpetrator of physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*). The phrase "attains the world of Śakra" is to be supplied in every case. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) concerning the prohibition against women, following the discussion on thieves and others. (8.386)
The suppression of these five within his own realm by a king brings him imperial power over his kinsmen and confers glory upon him in the world. (8.387)

Sovereignty (*sāmrājya*) consists in the power over the lives of others and independence. Regarding "among those of the same lineage" (*sajātyeṣu*): kings who are equal rivals are intended by the term "those of the same lineage. He stands at their head; the meaning is that they become executors of his commands. And in the world, they produce fame and renown for him. In both cases, it is precisely punishment that acts as the cause; even when people say, "This man is wrathful and a slayer of men," they are in fact praising him. (8.387)

If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—provided that each is capable of the ritual work and free from fault—the punishment for both of them shall be one hundred [paṇas]. (8.388)

The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is the performer of the ritual acts in a sacrifice, such as the *hotṛ*, *udgātṛ*, and others. Although that designation applies from the time after his selection until the completion of the performance, nevertheless, this rule does not concern the non-abandonment of one another by two who have already begun the rite; rather, it concerns the period prior to the selection. The usage of the term "officiating priest" is based on past status. One who has been selected for one performance is the very same person who is capable of being selected for another performance. This non-abandonment applies not only to one previously chosen, but also to his father and other ancestors. For thus says Nārada: "One who was previously accepted, or chosen by oneself" (NSm 3.10). Nor is this a restriction pertaining to a single individual; rather, it is a family custom (*kuladharma*). And so it is explained in detail in the *Mahābhārata* regarding Saṃvarta and Marutta. Therefore, those same priests who were chosen by the fathers and others of that lineage must be chosen.

This same rule applies even to those who officiate as priests (*yājana*). They too must engage such persons. If one desiring to sacrifice does not choose a priest (*ṛtvij*) who has already performed his priestly duties or someone else from that same lineage, but instead solicits another priest—one who is capable for the ritual, knowledgeable in its application, and free from defects such as being accused of crimes or having physical deficiencies—then if such a priest, when thus solicited, does not accept the office of officiating, provided the patron is faultless (not afflicted by these aforementioned defects), capable, and learned; in the event of such a rejection by either party, the fine is one hundred [paṇas]. The priest abandoning the patron shall be made to pay one hundred, and the patron abandoning the priest shall likewise pay one hundred.

This duty belongs not only to the officiating priest and the sacrificer, but also to the student and the teacher. Thus says Gautama: "Now, the non-sacrificing priest and the teacher [are to be abandoned]; they are also to be abandoned for serving one who has fallen from his caste. One falls by abandoning [them] otherwise" (GDh 21.12–13). Some maintain that this same duty applies to the giver and the recipient as well in the case of receiving a gift. 8.388.
Neither mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son deserves to be abandoned. One who abandons these, provided they have not fallen from their status, shall be fined six hundred by the king. (8.389)

A mother does not deserve abandonment; she is not to be cast off. Abandonment consists in expelling her from one's own home when she has failed in her conduct toward her son, provided that her service and assistance have been rendered without cause. This same principle should be explained for fathers and others as well, due to their connection with the term "kinship" (*saṃbandha*). In this context, by association, the word "woman" refers specifically to the wife. There is no abandonment of these persons unless they have fallen [from their caste]. Regarding the mother, Śātātapa states: "Some say that a mother does not fall [from her status] toward her son. As for the wife, abandonment means the cessation of sexual intercourse and the prohibition of her participation in household duties; however, the provision of food, clothing, and so forth is not forbidden. Thus it is recited: "Even when women have fallen [from virtue], food, clothing, and drink must be given, and they should dwell near the house" (MDh 11.187). 8.389.
When twice-born men in their hermitages dispute with one another over a matter,
a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to uphold righteousness should not issue a contrary judgment.

[318] Regarding the duty (*kārya*) and the law (*dharma*) pertaining to the hermitages of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and others who reside in forest retreats—when they are disputing with one another as to whether "this is the meaning of the scripture" or "this is not"—he should not hastily declare a settlement of their legal dispute, nor should he issue a decision by his own authority as if he were a sovereign over others. How then? In the manner that will be described below. In this way, he acts for his own welfare; the meaning is that he does not abandon the true purpose of the scriptures. This same method of decision applies even to householders when they are in the state of a religious order (*āśramin*). "Duty" refers to a subject of dispute consisting of a doubt regarding dharma. And by the mention of "hermitages," the specific scope of the rule is explained. (8.390)
Having honored these men as was appropriate along with the Brahmins, the king, having first pacified them with gentle words, should cause them to return to their own duty. (8.391)

[320] He now explains how that should be performed: having honored in exactly the same manner each person according to the kind of worship they deserve based on their qualities—by means of Brahmins, ministers, domestic priests, and so forth, whether in the performance of the worship or in the proclamation of the Dharma—one should then understand those Brahmins to be "truthful" (satya). Together with them, one should make known one's own duty (*svadharma*) and what is right and meaningful. Once his greatness has been established, the instruction to the members of the assembly is for the sake of preeminence; one should place them at the forefront. For instance, people do not become angry with a king through mere scriptural authority. Having first pacified them with words of affection and praise, and having thus removed their anger, one should then speak. (8.391)
If a Brahmin does not feed his neighbor or next-door neighbor when twenty worthy twice-born men are invited for a auspicious rite, he deserves a fine of one māṣaka. (8.392)

"Veśa" means a dwelling, that is, an abode; one who has gone toward that is a "prativeśa," meaning facing the house. One who exists there is a "prativeśya" (neighbor). In the reading with the initial long vowel (*prātiveśya*), the suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense. Similarly, an "anuveśya" is said to be one who dwells behind [the house]. If he should not feed those two—if, having brought them to his own home during a festive occasion such as a marriage where about twenty other twice-born men and others are fed—then he shall be made to pay a fine of one *māṣaka* of gold. This is understood from the qualification "gold" (*hiraṇya*) mentioned later; therefore, it applies here as well. If those two, the neighbor and the one living behind, are "arhau"—that is, if they are worthy, neither hostile nor utterly devoid of merit—[then this rule applies]. (8.392)
If those learned in the Vedas do not feed a virtuous fellow Vedic scholar at auspicious rites, they shall be made to pay double the value of that food and one *māṣaka* of gold. (8.393)

This undertaking is for the sake of those who do not live as neighbors; it is a rule for fellow students of the Veda (*sabrahmacārin*). A learned man (*śrotriya*) who does not feed another such learned man who is likewise virtuous at "prosperous rites" (*bhūtikṛtya*)—where "prosperity" (*bhūti*) means wealth and "rites" are those performed when such wealth exists, such as communal feasts and the like—or alternatively, where the term "prosperous" qualifies the rites themselves, meaning those grand ceremonies like weddings where more than twenty people are fed—at such festivals, he who fails to feed him shall be made to give him twice as much food intended for that purpose. Or else, he shall pay either gold or a *māṣaka* coin to the king. (8.393)

One who is blind, mentally deficient, a cripple who moves about on a board, one who is seventy years old and infirm, and one who renders service to those learned in the Vedas—none of these shall be made to pay a tax by anyone. (8.394)

The instrumental case in *saptatyā* is used in the sense of an inherent quality, as in the expression *prakṛtyā virūpaḥ* ("naturally deformed"). One who has lived for seventy years since birth is thus described. By serving those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyas*)—that is, those who study the Vedas—either through personal attendance such as massaging their feet or by performing manual labor, these [artisans] are not to be made to pay [taxes] by anyone, according to the rule: "Artisans [shall be exempt] month after month" (MDh 7.138). The phrase "by anyone" implies that they are not to be made to pay even by one whose treasury is depleted. (8.394)
The king should always honor a learned Vedic scholar, those afflicted by illness or pain, children, the elderly, the destitute, those of noble lineage, and the virtuous. 8.395

"Honoring" (*saṃpūjana*) means "favoring" (*anugraha*), because verbal roots have multiple meanings. For children and others, no other form of honoring is appropriate. They record in their tradition that the term *śrotriya* here refers specifically to a Brāhmaṇa. "The afflicted" (*ārta*) is one suffering from separation from loved ones and the like. "The destitute" (*akiñcana*) is one who is poor. "Of noble birth" (*mahākulīna*): one born into a family renowned for wealth, learning, valor, and other such qualities is "of noble birth. "Noble" (*ārya*) is one of upright nature, not crooked. One should show favor to these [persons] through gifts, honor, and so forth. Some explain "the destitute" as a qualifying attribute of "one of noble birth. (8.395)
On a smooth board made of *śālmalī* wood, a washerman should wash clothes slowly;
he should not rub garments against one another, nor should he let them dry together. (8.396)

The *śālmalī* is a tree; a board made from its wood is called a *śālmalī-phalaka*. For it is smooth by its very nature, and its fibers do not come loose even when the clothes are rubbed against it; for if they were to come loose, they would tear the garment. This restriction regarding the species of wood is not intended for some unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, there is no fault if another piece of wood with such a nature is used for the board. It must be smooth and not rough. One should not carry away the clothes belonging to one person by means of the clothes belonging to another. Having tied them up or wrapped them around, one should not take them to a bathing place to wash them, lest the clothes be destroyed by the tying; for they become excessively damaged when squeezed. Nor should one "wear" (*vāsayet*) them: one should not give clothes belonging to another to someone else, nor should one give them for the purpose of wearing in exchange for a price. For this is what "wearing" means: another wears them, and the washerman causes him to wear them. Since no specific punishment has been mentioned, the fine previously established in *māṣakas* should be applied here. (8.396)
A weaver shall give back ten palas of thread increased by one pala;
if he acts otherwise, he shall be made to pay a fine of twelve [paṇas]. (8.397)

A weaver, a *kuvinda*, weaves cloth; he is the maker of garments such as those for carts and the like. Having taken ten *palas* of thread, while weaving a garment, he should give back a cloth weighing one *pala* more. He should give everything with this rate of increase. This calculation should be applied to coarse and fine fabrics, as well as to those made of wool. Otherwise, there shall be a fine of twelve *paṇas*. This fine applies in the case of not providing the increase; however, in the case of cutting off the principal amount, that which has been stated in the list [of fines] applies. Thus, if he does not provide the increase for twenty *palas*, the fine shall be double. The calculation should be made in this manner: triple, quadruple, and so forth.
Others, however, say that the "staff" refers to the king's share. (8.397)
Those skilled at customs stations and expert in evaluating all merchandise shall determine the price according to the goods; from that, the king shall take one-twentieth as tax. (8.398)

Those places where tolls are collected are called *śulkasthānāni* (toll-stations), established by kings or merchants as fixed for their respective regions. In those places, those who are skilled customs officers (*śaulkika*)—who cannot be deceived by rogues, and who are discerning experts knowing the methods regarding the arrival, purchase, sale, loss, expenditure, quality, and worthlessness of all commodities—should determine the value of the goods that have arrived from another country or are being transported away. From that, the king shall take a twentieth part.
What, then, is the use of calculating the value? It should simply be stated that it is one-twentieth of the merchandise.

True; when the king takes the substance according to its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), items such as cloth and the like are utilized in their original state. In that case, a twentieth part [as tax] prior to the twentieth [unit] would not be possible without cutting [the fabric]; for this purpose, the determination of value (*arghakaraṇa*) is established. This is to make known that there is no toll (*śulka*) on goods that are not for sale but for one's own personal use, according to the nature of the merchandise. Likewise, it is according to the suitability of the time. Not every commodity is sold at all times at a uniform price. Therefore, the determination of the value of commodities depends upon place and time; the price is not fixed. (8.398)
If one, out of greed, exports those articles of the king that are renowned or prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire property. (8.399)

Those goods renowned for their association with a king because of their utility to royalty—such as elephants; saffron in Kashmir; silk, wool, and the like in the eastern regions; horses in the western regions; and gems, pearls, and so forth in the southern regions—whatever is easily obtained in the territory of a particular king but rare elsewhere, that is what is proclaimed there. For by means of such items, kings enter into mutual alliances. Prohibited goods are those which the king has declared: "This shall not be taken from my country to another place, or it must be sold only here," such as grain during a famine and so on. If someone, out of greed, exports them to another country or sells them, the king shall confiscate everything; "sarvahāra" means the seizure of all property. This is the punishment for one who takes them away out of a desire for wealth. However, if they are intended as a gift to another king, the punishment is even more severe, including corporal penalties such as confinement within a fortress and the like. (8.399)
One who evades a customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
or one who gives false accounts in the reckoning of goods, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty.

A merchant who buys and sells is called a *vāṇijaka*. If he avoids the customs station (*śulkasthāna*) by taking a wrong path, or goes at an improper time—such as at night when the customs officials have departed—and speaks falsely regarding the count, stating a lower number during the enumeration; and since this "counting" is illustrative, this same rule applies even in cases of concealment. He shall be made to pay an eightfold fine for the offense (*atyaya*). He is to be made to pay eight times as much as what he has concealed, or eight times the amount of duty (*śulka*) that would have been appropriate for that which was concealed. The former interpretation alone is more reasonable, for the word "offense" (*atyaya*) is applicable there, since the substance [of the goods] is the cause of that [offense].

Others, however, connect the phrase as "those who buy and sell at an improper time. And this prohibition regarding an improper time applies when the toll has not been paid or when the transaction takes place in secret. (8.400)
Having investigated the importation, exportation, and storage, as well as both the increase and decrease of all commodities, he should regulate their purchase and sale. (8.401)

Those who are sellers in the marketplace shall not be permitted to set the price according to their own will, nor shall the king purchase at a price fixed by his own preference. How then? This and that must be investigated: [361] the source—whether it returns from another country or not, and likewise from how far away it comes; likewise at the point of exit—whether it is sold immediately or remains stored. For a commodity exiting at this moment, even a small profit is of great consequence; furthermore, there is profit through further buying and selling of other goods using the proceeds arising from that [initial sale]. Regarding increase and decrease at the location: how much increase remains for it, or what kind of decrease occurs. Having examined all this, he should arrange buying and selling within his own country. He should fix the price in such a way that there is no oppression of either the merchants or the buyers. (8.401)
Every five nights, or else every fortnight when it has passed, the king should perform the ritual offering of the guest-water (argha) in their presence. (8.402)

Because substances subject to arrival and departure are impermanent, there is an increase and decrease in their value that takes many forms. Therefore, the fixing of prices must be verified every five nights; it should not be considered as having been done once and for all, nor should one place trust in merchants. Rather, one must exercise personal vigilance. Regarding a commodity that remains in stock for a long time, the search for its price should be conducted every fortnight; in other cases, it should be done every five nights. (8.402)
All weights, measures, and standards of measurement shall be well-defined;
and every six months, they must be re-examined. (8.403)

The *tulā* (balance) is well known. *Māna* refers to measures such as the *prastha*, the *droṇa*, and so forth. *Pratīmāna* is that which is made for the purpose of determining the weight of gold and other substances; it must be well-marked on all sides and stamped with the royal insignia. Having determined [the weights] himself by direct observation, he should verify them with his own seal. Every six months, he should have a re-examination conducted by trustworthy officials so that no one may tamper with them. (8.403)
A vehicle shall be made to pay one paṇa at a ferry; a man, half a paṇa;
cattle and women, a quarter; and an empty-handed man, half a quarter. (8.404)

On a riverbank, a vehicle such as a cart or carriage must pay a *paṇa* for crossing. Since it will be taught later that this applies to those filled with goods, this royal share is for empty vehicles being brought across for the purpose of fetching goods. A load carried by men, when being brought for the purpose of fetching goods, must pay half a *paṇa*. An animal, such as a cow or a buffalo, and a woman, must pay one-quarter (*pāda*). One who is empty pays nothing. That man who has taken up a load must pay half a quarter (*pādārdha*). Because an empty man is presumed to have the capacity to cross the river on his own, he is treated lightly and the levy is small. A woman, due to her lack of strength, is made to pay more for crossing herself. This refers to the fee for crossing. (8.404)
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay a ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, and men without belongings, shall pay whatever little they can. (8.405)

"Goods" (*bhāṇḍa*) refers to wealth such as clothing, grain, and so forth. Vessels filled with these must be made to pay the crossing fee according to their value for the purpose of crossing. If expensive items such as clothing have been loaded there in great quantity, then they must be made to pay much; however, if it is not excessively heavy due to grain and the like, then they pay little. In this manner, the assessment should be made based on whether the river is easy or difficult to cross. Empty vessels must pay a small fraction of a *paṇa*. Here, the word "goods" (*bhāṇḍa*) denotes wealth. As for those who are without belongings (*aparicchada*), they do not pay half a *pāda*, but rather some amount more or less than that. No fixed rule is possible in this matter; therefore, discretionary assessment alone is the intended meaning of the scripture. (8.405)
On a long journey, one should know that a crossing may be found according to the location and the time, such as on the banks of rivers; however, there is no such sign at the ocean.

First, regarding the crossing of the near and far shores (*pārāvārottāraṇa*): this refers to traveling from one village to another by boat. Regarding the long journey to be traversed by a measure such as a *yojana*: "according to the place" means that whatever ferry-fare has been established by the ferrymen in a particular location, that very amount must be paid. "According to the time": time refers to the rainy season and so forth when there is much water; in such cases, the price is different. When a river has little water and a village is reached only after a long time, the ferrymen, being more fatigued, may charge a higher price. The word *tara* (crossing) is used here for the cause in the sense of the effect; thus, *tara* would mean the fare. To the extent that the distance is long, to that same extent the ferry-fare increases. This should be understood to apply to the banks of rivers. On the ocean or the great sea, there is no characteristic of crossing (*tara-lakṣaṇa*). It is not possible to determine how many *yojanas* the boat has been hauled so that the price could be calculated accordingly. On rivers and streams, it is possible to know, "this path is one *yojana* long" or "two *yojanas*. For in those places, villages serve as markers of measurement. In that case, whatever the price is for a one-*yojana* journey, it becomes double for a two-*yojana* journey. But on the ocean, the boat carries a great load, and it is not at all possible to determine the measurement in *yojanas* and so forth. Therefore it is said: "On the ocean, there is no characteristic [of crossing]. (8.406)
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as an ascetic, a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll at a crossing. (8.407)

After two months, a woman whose menstrual period has ceased becomes one whose pregnancy is manifest; because she is worthy of favor, the ferry-toll should not be taken from her. A *pravrajita* is one belonging to the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*). A *muni* is an ascetic (*tāpasa*). *Brāhmaṇas* are those who bear the marks [of their order], such as celibate students (*brahmacārin*). The mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is a qualification; therefore, this rule does not apply to those who merely wear the external marks of renunciation. The purpose of crossing is the "ferry-toll" (*tārika*), consisting of a *paṇa* or other fees; they are not to be made to pay for the sake of crossing. Although the word *tārika* alone would have sufficed according to the requirements of the meter, the term *tara* is used for metrical reasons. (8.407)
Whatever may be lost on a ship through the fault of the boatmen must be paid back by those very boatmen, having assembled together from their own respective shares. (8.408)

If merchandise not loaded onto a boat is lost due to the fault of the ferrymen or sailors—either because they lead it through a place with swirling waters while knowing the location, or because they fail to enter the water with firm lashings, or because they have loosened the wind-ropes by means of iron rings, leather thongs, or cordage—and if the goods are thereby shattered or destroyed, then those very ferrymen must pay for them from their own respective shares; that is, all the ferrymen who boarded the boat shall assemble and pay the owner of the goods from their individual portions. (8.408)
This has been declared as the legal decision regarding those traveling by boat:
for damage in the water caused by the fault of the boatmen, there is no punishment; however, in the case of an act of God (an accident), there is no liability.

Those whose livelihood is by boat travel by means of ships; for them, this rule is declared: whatever is lost in the water due to the fault of the boatmen, that they shall pay. In the case of a divine calamity or a sudden accident, such as the breaking of the ship by wind and so forth, there is no penalty for the boatmen for the loss of goods.

This is the rule for carriers of goods or porters on land: if a porter proceeds with care, holding onto his staff, while the upper part of his load is firmly bound, and the goods should by chance be destroyed when he falls on a muddy path seen [only] at the last moment, there shall be no fault on the part of the porter. (8.409)
One should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, money-lending, and agriculture, as well as the tending of cattle; and the Śūdra [should perform] service for the twice-born. (8.410)

On this point, some explain as follows: "Even if they are unwilling, the Vaiśya and the Śūdra must have those duties performed by force, because this is their own specific duty (*svadharma*). Even though there is a visible purpose, an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*) exists because it is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). And if this were the case, it would follow that even a Brāhmaṇa should be made to accept gifts by force. If it is argued that this [consequence] was stated as a flaw only for that particular position, here too, this very same position holds.

That is incorrect. When there is a desire for wealth, the restriction is based on the scripture; however, activity is not necessarily bound by an injunction (*vidhi*). Where one has a personal motive, an injunction does not function as the instigator. The operation of the injunction, however, lies in the aspect of restriction (*niyama*). Such is this restriction: one should cause only a Vaiśya to engage in trade, and one who performs it otherwise when no distress exists should be punished. Likewise, [one should cause] only a Brāhmaṇa to accept gifts. And thus it follows that even though he is capable of accepting gifts, he should remain devoted to contentment. As for what is heard in the text, "even against his will" (MDh 8.412), that is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*). In all such cases, the form of a restriction is to be understood as "only a Śūdra [should perform] servitude. (8.410)
A Brāhmaṇa should support with compassion both a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties. (8.411)

A Brāhmaṇa who has been emaciated by his livelihood should support them with gifts of food and the like; he should provide for the maintenance of both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. Out of benevolence—that is, out of compassion—he should cause them to perform their own respective duties: those which are the Brāhmaṇa’s own, such as fetching sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, and water-jars; or else those which are the Kṣatriya’s and the Vaiśya’s own. The Kṣatriya should be appointed to tasks such as guarding the village, and the Vaiśya to his own work, such as agriculture and the tending of cattle. This rule applies specifically to a Brāhmaṇa who possesses great wealth and a large retinue, as inferred from the context. Because of the expression "their own duties," they must not be made to perform servile labor, such as cleaning away contemptible leavings and the like. (8.411)
If a Brāhmaṇa, out of greed and by virtue of his superior power, compels initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will, he shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (8.412)

They have been consecrated and initiated. Although this is already understood from the mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*) alone, it is nevertheless stated for the purpose of indicating the three castes (*traivarṇika*). A Brāhmaṇa who, by virtue of his power—the state of being powerful (*prābhavyam*), which is sovereignty—compels those of the same caste who are unwilling to perform servitude consisting of washing feet, clearing away food-leavings, sweeping, and so forth, shall be fined six hundred [paṇas]. This is on account of greed; however, if it is done out of hatred or other motives, he shall be punished more severely. The form *prābhavyāt* is derived from the present participle (*śatṛnta*) of the root *bhū* with an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). Because of the expression "by virtue of power," there is no fault in the case of a teacher. Because of the expression "unwilling," a different punishment applies to those who are willing. (8.412)
But a Śūdra, whether purchased or even unpurchased, one should make perform service;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa. (8.413)

"Acquired" means purchased; "unacquired" means obtained as alms-food and so forth. This is a restatement of the rule that is about to be taught. The phrase "only for the purpose of service" is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). || 8.413 ||
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that [status] is innate to him, so who can remove it from him? (8.414)

Even though he has been released by one who relied upon him through the seven modes of servitude, and even though he is freed from that [status], who can remove—that is, take away—that innate, co-natal, and inherent servitude from that Śūdra? Just as the Śūdra caste cannot be removed from him, so too servitude cannot be removed. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), because the author will later state that there is release from servitude for a Śūdra under specific circumstances. (8.414)

One captured under a banner, one who is a slave for food, one born in the house, one purchased, one inherited, one enslaved by way of a fine, and one inherited from an ancestor—these seven are the origins of slavery. (8.415)
The mention of the "banner" (*dhvaja*) is intended to indicate the vehicle (*vāhana*). An army is called *dhvajinī*. "Brought from there" means having been conquered in battle and reduced to slavery.
But is this a statement regarding a Kṣatriya—that a Kṣatriya conquered in battle becomes a slave?

We say no; for it is the Śūdra who is the subject under discussion, as [the text] states: "He was created solely for servitude" (MDh 8.413). Having defeated the master, the slave belonging to him is brought away. He enters into the state of slavery of the one who brought him.

But is it not the case that servitude has been specifically prescribed for the Śūdra alone, as in: "That [servitude] is innate to him" (MDh 8.414)? It is not so; for if that were the case, there would be a lack of regulation, as it would remain unknown who his master is. Indeed, all members of the three higher castes would then be liable to be his slaves. Furthermore, for one who follows his own duty (*svadharma*), there is no fixed rule because there is no specific injunction.
Others, however, maintain that servitude exists even for Kṣatriyas and others, based on the rule: "And all [castes] should serve each other in the order of their sequence" (GDh 10.66).

That is incorrect; servitude is one thing and service is another. Servitude consists in being made to perform lowly tasks by one who is unknown, and in the absence of any restriction for one sent on all errands. Service, however, consists in massaging the body and the authority to protect wealth, wives, and so forth. This has been explained in detail by Nārada (NSm 5.24–42).

A *bhaktadāsa* (slave for food) is one who has entered into servitude for the sake of obtaining food. A *gṛhaja* (born-in-the-house) is one born in the house. A *garbhadāsa* (slave from the womb) is one produced from a female slave. A *krīta* (purchased) is one bought from a master for a price. A *datrima* (given) is one given out of affection or for some unseen spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). A *kramāgata* (inherited) is one belonging to the paternal line. Now, what is the distinction between this *gṛhaja* and the other? The *gṛhaja* is born of that very master’s own female slave, whereas the other is inherited through the lineage. A *daṇḍadāsa* (slave for punishment) is one who, being unable to pay a fine to the king, is made a slave.
Regarding the statement, "One may also make [him] equal by means of labor" (MDh 8.177), some maintain that even one of lower caste may be made a slave.

That is incorrect; for slavery is one thing, and being compelled to perform labor is another. Furthermore, this is not a punishment through which [slavery] would be included. Nor has the maintenance of a person born into the state of slavery been mentioned here, since the text says only "also by means of labor. Likewise, there exists the labor of a slave. But surely, even a Śūdra who has come [to serve] through religious duty (dharma) is considered a slave; in that case, how can there be only seven origins of slavery?

This is not a fault. His status as a slave is not innate, because he acts according to his own will when seeking merit (*dharma*). For it is not appropriate for him to perform the acts of giving or lending [money], just like slaves who are purchased or born in the house. Thus it has been said: "In whatever way he follows the conduct of the virtuous... (MDh 10.128). By saying this, it is demonstrated that his servitude is not permanent; rather, it is for one who desires a specific reward. Consequently, there is no servitude for one who lacks such desire. Therefore, if a Śūdra possesses wealth and lives independently without depending on Brāhmaṇas or others, he would never be at fault. (8.415)
A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong. 8.416

These three, though they have acquired wealth, are yet without property; the wealth belongs to the master. Whatever wealth they acquire, that wealth belongs to him under whose ownership they have come—the wife’s wealth belongs to the husband, the son’s to the father, and the slave’s to the master.

But surely, if these [women] are without property, how can they have entitlement through their own ritual acts? In that case, this would not be tenable: "If the two sons should be maintainers of the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the son should give to those same persons to whom the father gave. Furthermore, the joint duty of husband and wife must be performed: "In matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, you must not be transgressed by her. And if she is without property, what else could "non-transgression regarding artha" mean? Even for a Śūdra, the rule "he should sacrifice himself with *pākayajñas*" (GDh 10.65) would be contradicted if he were without property. One might argue that there is no contradiction because this refers to a Śūdra who acts according to his own will; however, slaves certainly possess ownership over their own wealth, since they are designated as having "their own wealth. For there can be no designation of something as one's own when no such relationship exists. Moreover, it is a contradiction to say that acquisition does not produce ownership. Therefore, the claim that "what they acquire is not their own" is contradictory—just like someone saying, "She whose son I am, she is not my mother. Or, if women lacked ownership, scriptural passages such as "the sacrifice is performed only with the consent of the wife" and "the wife indeed has authority over the household goods" (MS 3.7.9) would be without foundation.

To this it is replied: this is a prescription regarding dependence. In the absence of the husband’s permission, women must not independently employ their wealth for any purpose whatsoever. The same should be understood to apply to sons and slaves as well. Others, however, hold that the mention of wife and son is intended to include the slave; and this statement is for the sake of what follows: in times of distress, one should have no hesitation in taking their wealth, for that property belongs to the husband alone. (8.416)
A Brāhmaṇa may confidently take property from a Śūdra;
for he has nothing of his own, as his wealth is to be taken by his master. (8.417)
And thus someone has said: "This refers to the domain of Śūdras who have attained the Dharma.

That has been stated because there is no evidence for a specific restriction. Therefore, it is said that a Śūdra is the servant of everyone, and that he alone is the one from whom [gifts] may be accepted.

"Confidently" means without hesitation. One should not entertain the doubt, "How can I accept the wealth of a Śūdra? For that is forbidden," because it is said that he has no property of his own for which he might have an accumulation. His wealth is taken by his master, the owner; this alone is the purpose of its acquisition—that the master takes it. Therefore, one may confidently take up or seize property. Even if it is not being formally offered, one may employ it as if it were in one's own house. This is appropriate when there is a need. There is no fault for one who lacks wealth and accepts [gifts] from a Śūdra slave. (8.417)
One should cause the Vaiśyas and Śūdras to perform their own duties with diligence; for if they fall away from their respective duties, they would throw this world into turmoil. (8.418)

If they were to transgress their duties, they might disturb and throw the world into confusion; therefore, they must not be permitted to deviate from their own tasks through any effort. Even Vaiśyas, upon committing a significant transgression, should indeed be subjected to severe punishment. There is no imprisonment for them, for their own dharma can be maintained through the power of wealth alone. (8.418)
Day by day he should inspect his undertakings and his mounts, as well as his fixed income and expenditure, his mines, and his treasury. (8.419)

For the purpose of maintaining the royal duties: "enterprises" refers to agriculture, customs stations, and so forth; "vehicles" refers to elephants and the like; "income and expenditure" must be constantly investigated as follows: "this has been received by him, this has been disbursed"; "mines" are lands where ores such as gold are produced; and "treasury" is the place for the accumulation of wealth. (8.419)
Thus, by settling all these legal cases, the king, having cast off all evil, attains the supreme goal. || 8.420 ||

By settling legal disputes, such as those concerning debts and the like, in the manner described—that is, bringing them to a conclusion through a formal decision—he casts off and removes all that is tainted by unknown defects; having dispelled his sin, he attains and reaches the supreme goal, the desired realm of heaven or liberation. || 8.420 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "General Judicial Procedure," in the section on the Duties of Kings within the *Saṃhitā* of the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra* proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
